#1296. Inside the crime epidemic striking fear into Premier League stars: Terrified players paying 'protection money' and buying £20,000 guard dogs, WAGs targeted in violent carjackings and the fall of the crime family who targeted Alexander Isak

Published: 12:00 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 04:24 EST, 20 November 2026

The man parked up in a nondescript green Ford Fiesta cut an incongruous sight in the affluent residential neighbourhood of Casal Palocco, in south-west Rome, but no one paid him much notice. He made no eye contact and at no stage stepped from the car.

It was only after the street’s famous resident, AS Roma’s Belgian midfielder Radja Nainggolan, had his home burgled and an extraordinary £400,000 worth of possessions stolen that the player’s then wife, Claudia, six months pregnant at that time in April 2016, recalled the Eastern European-looking man in the battered vehicle up their street.

He was Vlada Djuric, a 50-year-old Macedonian of Romani descent and part of the wider Nikolov family, including his wife Zora Jovanovic, their two sons and daughter, whose highly organised thefts from the homes of top footballers would continue for more than a decade, with imprisonment deemed only a minor setback.

While the Nainggolans were blithely unaware of the criminal family’s lookout man – they’d gone to visit friends nearby for a couple of hours and hadn't even bothered to activate the burglar alarm – the assailants were primed to seize the chance.

The two sons, Valentino and Giacomo, mounted the villa’s perimeter wall, opening one door with a magnetic card and jimmying another with a screwdriver, and proceeded undisturbed through the house in 27 minutes, throwing the proceeds of their burglary into a bag as they went.

There were 15 watches (Rolex, Patek Philippe and others) valued at £250,000 and 20 pieces of jewellery, including a diamond worth £25,000. Security cameras on a landing and in an internal room filmed them but such was their confidence, they only partially covered their faces.

Former Roma midfielder Radja Nainggolan and his then wife Claudia, who was six months pregnant, were the targets of a burglary in 2016 (Source: Instagram/Claudia_lai_82)

Nainggolan had an extraordinary £400,000 worth of possessions taken, including 15 watches

It was old-fashioned detective work from a local officer, Bruno Failla, which led police to a rambling home at Lurano, a small town six hours drive away in Lombardy, at which the Nikolovs would lavishly entertain other members of the Romani community.

The watches matched the descriptions of those stolen from the Nainggolans, though it was a necklace with a Roma logo, and the pair of red shoes with Nainggolan's initials, which really gave the game away.

‘I ask again for vigilance and watchfulness, please,’ Failla said at the time, because this was the fourth time that footballers' properties in Casal Palocco had been targeted in the space of five years. But the challenge of placing footballers in a state of constant vigilance became clear fully seven years on, when another Nainggolan residence, in Antwerp, Belgium, was burgled while his relatives held a party there.

‘It is one of the most complicated and consistently challenging parts of our security work,’ one former special forces soldier now providing security for footballers tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘It’s been a big sector of our work for years now, but the movements of these clients are so public and that’s irresistible to criminals. The wealth is very evident.’

One of the sons, Valentino, was jailed for two years in 2016 and other members of his family also did time, but once out, they all set their sights on the Premier League. In 2024, they arrived in the UK via a ferry to Dover from Calais, stopped off in London and made their way north, sleeping in a Ford motorhome and travelling to target homes in a Citroen C3.

A spree of attacks ensued from them on the homes of Alexander Isak, then a Newcastle player, Wolves’ Matheus Cunha (who has subsequently been burgled again while at Manchester United), Birmingham City’s Neil Etheridge and Leon Bailey, with Aston Villa at the time.

A number of Premier League clubs, including Liverpool, Everton and United, are known to have appointed their own security teams to provide an around-the-clock presence at the homes of players who are in squads playing away from home – rather than have that in the hands of a range of private operators.

Some of the top football TV analysts are known to have sought the same security cover outside their houses when away at games.

A number of Premier League clubs, including Liverpool, have appointed their own security teams to provide an around-the-clock presence at the homes of stars who are playing away

Three masked criminals managed to slip over Bruno Fernandes' security fence and into his home in Nether Alderley, Cheshire, last month and made off with jewellery

It didn’t work in the case of Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes. Three masked criminals still managed to slip over the security fence into his home in Nether Alderley, Cheshire, last month and make off with jewellery.

It was one of the player’s neighbours who spotted them on their CCTV system and alerted police, who arrived five minutes after the burglars had left. Some in this security sector feel that it takes the private firms' former military and special services experience to cope with the criminal gangs’ level of sophistication.

Clubs using security staff in this way is a relatively recent development. In the days of security officers like United’s Ned Kelly, who wrote a book about his 14 years with the club, the job entailed ensuring the team were protected in public, or ferrying managers and new signings around.

Many clubs still leave it to players. ‘Player-liaison staff will recommend vetted security providers but it’s down to player personal choice for obvious reasons,’ says one player agent.

'That's not always been easy,' says a former Premier League player-liaison officer. 'The players have a huge entourage: so-called experts who want a seat at the table and think they know best. Of course, social media enhances the security problem.'

The house burglars’ modus operandi pales by comparison with some of violence displayed by others who prey on the footballer set. One footballer's wife in Cheshire was driving a top-of-the-range vehicle when a moped took up a position in front of her and slowed. In her rear-view mirror, she saw a second. The driver of the third then arrived at her side window, assessing what there was to steal.

On any given day, there could have been £200,000 worth of jewellery in the car, though she was wearing neither rings nor a watch on this occasion. The three drove off.

The episode had echoes of the attempted heist which saw Arsenal’s Mesut Ozil and Sead Kolasinac carjacked in broad daylight in north London, seven years ago.

Sead Kolasinac, then of Arsenal, thwarts an attempted carjacking in broad daylight in north London, seven years ago. Kolasinac was with his team-mate Mesut Ozil at the time

Attackers go for Kolasinac after his car was 'boxed in' when approaching traffic lights

Paul Hughes, managing director of Benchmark Security Group, a leading Manchester-based protection firm, employs former police and Royal security drivers to train his clients in the art of 'defensive driving'.

In a two-hour session, they learn how to avoid being 'boxed in' – as Ozil and Kolasinac were – when approaching traffic lights. Techniques include never taking up a position in the middle lane, avoiding the outside lane if there is a central barrier, and always maintaining sight of the tyres of the vehicle in front when you slow.

'If you can see the tyres, you will always have room to manoeuvre right or left of the car in front, at speed, without hitting it,' Hughes says.

His staff are often asked to escort clients in their fleet of vehicles, which includes two Land Rovers with blacked-out windows. The firm acquired a Darkfighter Dome – a night-vision camera which is mounted on to the roof of its security vehicles – allowing them to see would-be assailants in the dark. Escorted school runs are also part of the protection they offer.

A screen which dominates Benchmark's underground headquarters, at anonymous premises in Manchester, revealed the fortresses that players' houses have become, when I visited.

It showed live feeds from the gardens of mansions which are criss-crossed by infra-red beams. An alarm is triggered in the control room if anyone not approved through face-recognition software is picked up by up to 18 pan, tilt and zoom cameras at a property.

Loudspeakers, operated from the control room, warn off intruders. A team of security staff is never more than six minutes away. A patrol is on the scene of an alert, usually within 90 seconds.

A number of Manchester United players have invested in specialised security dogs from the Leicester-based firm Chaperone K9 at a cost of up to £20,000 each, though some sources suggest demand has receded as many players have young children. Security firms have their own dogs.

Benchmark are one of Britain's most trusted operators – industry-accredited, with former senior police officers on their staff. But this is also a world in which some unsavoury individuals are looking to extract gain.

Daily Mail Sport is aware that a number of current players have paid protection money to ensure they remain safe and are not venturing out socially without having done so. The ‘panic rooms’ some install in their homes, with security card access, are a place to hide valuables.

The family who preyed on footballers for a decade will be behind bars for some time. Valentino Nikolov (pictured) is serving an initial 10-year sentence, which has since been extended

Kolasinac fought off the carjackers. Everton's Duncan Ferguson put an assailant in hospital when he tried to burgle his home at Ormskirk, Lancashire, in January 2001. ‘I’m not a hard man off the pitch...unless you try to break into my house,’ he said recently.

But the assailants in the Ozil and Kolasinac attack were part of Eastern European gangs. 'The criminal demographic has changed,' one former senior detective tells me. 'We are now talking about gangs who lack the slightest compunction about taking a life.'

The Italian family who have preyed on footballers for a decade will be behind bars for some time. The Rome lookout man’s two sons were jailed for 10 years and eight years respectively at Newcastle Crown Court last year, for burglaries including the Isak attack – sentences since extended. Their mother is doing seven years.

That court case revealed how the family had moved on from the days of old cars, screwdrivers and shinning over walls in Rome – using Isak’s own vehicle as a battering ram to force entry to his Newcastle home.

'None of the property stolen from my home was ever recovered,’ Isak related. 'The attack left me with a sense of unease and a fear it could reoccur.'

#1295. It's Over: Emery Calls Time on Garnacho's Aston Villa Career

Aston Villa were held to a 0-0 draw against Sunderland on Saturday afternoon in the Premier League as they returned to action following the international break.

The Villans were hoping to get back to winning ways after four games without a win in all competitions heading into this one, but the team struggled to create many clear-cut chances and failed to break down a Sunderland side sitting in the relegation zone before kick-off.

The goalless draw leaves the team in 11th place in the Premier League, having won just three of their opening 11 games in the top-flight this season, with Emery still looking to find the right balance after losing a host of key first-team stars during the summer transfer window.

But despite what happened on the pitch at Villa Park on Saturday afternoon, the biggest story was who wasn't around to see it take place.

When the starting lineups were announced 75 minutes before kick-off, Emery named a strong lineup which included Alysson and Emi Buendia on the wings, Johan Manzambi playing as a number ten, and Nicolas Jackson up front, with Boubacar Kamara and Leon Goretzka supporting them.

That meant there was only space on the bench for Ross Barkley, John McGinn, Joao Gomes, Ibrahim Mbaye, Brian Madjo, and George Hemmings. But more importantly, and perhaps significantly, there was no space whatsoever for summer signing Alejandro Garnacho.

Garnacho was the first attacking signing of the summer at Villa Park as Emery looked to replace Morgan Rogers following his move to Chelsea, but the Argentine has struggled to make any sort of impact.

In fact, he has managed just 96 minutes of action across all competitions so far this season, failing to start a single game. Emery has previously addressed his situation publicly, stating that he needed to do more.

"[He has to] continue working. Work, work, train, work. When he can have minutes to play, try and play well. He is progressing, but we have players in front of him now.

"We want a competitive team and players to compete in the style we have. Garnacho is a little bit behind, because of some circumstances we had in pre-season," Emery said. "It is time to be patient for the time he needs."

After the September international break, Emery claimed that he had improved, but he still managed just 64 minutes between that return to action and the most recent break.

Now he has been left out of the 20-man squad entirely, despite Matty Cash, Matteo Ruggeri and Amadou Onana all being unavailable due to injury, and that suggests that the Spaniard has made his mind up about his long-term future at Villa Park.

After causing trouble at Man Utd, the club decide to cut their losses and moved him on to Chelsea, but he quickly ran into problems there too. The club shipped him off after just one season, and Villa looked keen to revitalise his career.

However, even Emery can't work miracles this big, and it's clear that the winger simply needs to move away from the Premier League to have any chance of getting his career back on track.

Villa have too much to play for and too many options ahead of him to be giving him pity minutes, and he's clearly not doing enough in training to warrant an opportunity. With a season-long loan deal agreed with an obligation to join permanently based on certain conditions, this is a very familiar scenario for the club.

After the Harvey Elliott debacle last season, it's clear that they have learn their lesson. If the club are able to cancel the loan in January then they will surely look at doing that. If not, then the 22-year-old will have a long wait until the summer before moving on, because it's evident that he has no future at Aston Villa.

High-stakes January pursuit heats up as two Premier League clubs chase a lightning winger after national heroics.

#1294. Fiorentina coach Vanoli: ‘Ndour and Njie are fine, Atta is back’ ahead of Monza clash

Paolo Vanoli says Cher Ndour and Alieu Njie are both fit and Arthur Atta is back in contention as Fiorentina prepare to face Monza on Monday night.

With quotes via TuttoMercatoWeb, the Fiorentina coach gave his pre-match press conference at the Viola Park ahead of the trip to the U-Power Stadium, where kick-off is at 20:45 CET [19:45 GMT].

“Ndour has been training separately and will join the group tomorrow. Njie took a knock on international duty but has come back well and recovered,” Vanoli said. “Oulaï has come back well too, and his morale is high after his goal. Fagioli is in a different frame of mind, but he’s fired up. Atta has been training with the group, and I think he’ll be involved in Monza.

“He’s an important player and I’m happy to have him back, but he’s been out for a long time, so his minutes will increase gradually.”

Vanoli also responded to reports that he might free Franco Mastantuono from defensive duties.

“I’m sorry you’re spreading the idea that an attacker has to stay close to goal. That’s your speculation. Kvara said that if he didn’t defend, he didn’t play. Football today is about both phases. We need to get better so he does less defending by improving our attacking play, but a player has to be complete if he wants to stay at the very highest level. I’ve never seen a coach who doesn’t make a player do defensive work.”

Fiorentina are unbeaten in three after beating Sassuolo 4-2 and drawing 2-2 with Juventus. They’re 15th on nine points, two above Monza, who are 18th and have Serie A’s top scorer, Gustavo Varela.

“They’re well organised, with a very good coach. They’re a direct team who go man-to-man, so we’ll need to move the ball quickly without holding on to it too much. They’re top in almost every physical category, so it’ll be a complicated game. Every team that’s played there has suffered.”

Fiorentina have conceded 25 goals in 11 games, and Vanoli was asked about it.

“It’s not the same defence as last year. Apart from De Gea, all the others are new. Plenty of teams in Italian football concede more. We’re being brave, as we were against Juventus, but we need to work better on individual tactics at the back. That’s something that’s been lost a bit in Italy.”

Asked what he’d like for Christmas from the transfer market, he replied: “I’d choose a win against Monza.”

#1293. Observation of tunable superradiant frequency combs

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Cavity quantum electrodynamics1 with quantum emitters coupled to resonators provides a powerful platform for engineering light–matter interactions2,3 and exploring many-body phenomena4,5. In particular, superradiance6—arising from collective quantum interference among emitters—has been explored as a route to ultrastable continuous radiation7. However, engineering superradiance in the time domain to realize periodic pulsed sources or frequency combs remains largely unexplored. Here we investigate the non-equilibrium many-body dynamics of a driven spin ensemble coupled with an on-chip superconducting resonator and uncover a dynamical phase transition from continuous-wave to periodic pulsed superradiant emission. To quantitatively capture the observed dynamical phases, we introduce a driven-dissipative cavity-quantum electrodynamics model that elucidates how the periodic pulsed superradiant phase emerges from collective, periodically repeating spin dynamics stabilized by the interplay of coherence growth, disorder and dissipation. We also find that rare-earth ion spin systems with both optical and microwave transitions enable phase-synchronized, dual-rail superradiant frequency combs in both the microwave and the optical domains. Our results not only open new opportunities for atom-based frequency-comb sources and programmable superradiant generation, but establish a fundamental connection between periodic pulsed superradiance and the emergence of a continuous time crystal8,9,10 as a new non-equilibrium phase in driven open systems.

a, Detailed device schematic. A niobium film is patterned on a 500 μm thick 171Yb3+:YVO4 crystal. A 100 nm gold layer is evaporated on the back side, forming a weak optical Fabry-Pérot mode between the front and back chip reflections. b, Calibration of spin-cavity coupling strength. By optically pumping the population into the \(| \downarrow \rangle \) state, we probe the resonant spin-cavity coupling spectrum and its strength while avoiding superradiant effects. The blue data in the bottom subpanel correspond to the continuous-wave (CW) pump being off, while the black data are taken with a 400 μW continuous-wave pump. By fitting to a spin-cavity coupling model, we extract an ensemble coupling strength of \(\sqrt{N}g\approx 2\pi \times 1.1\) MHz, corresponding to a normalized coupling gnorm ≈ 0.6 < 1. The single-spin coupling, g = 2π × 10 Hz, and the effective ensemble size, N = 1010, are estimated from Comsol simulation and dopant concentration. c, Ensemble coupling strength, \(\sqrt{N}g\), as a function of pump power. We observe that the ensemble coupling strength increases with pump power, indicating a larger population in the microwave spin manifold.

a, A pulsed, transient optical pumping scheme that drives 171Yb3+ spins into the \(| \uparrow \rangle \) state. The resulting inverted spin polarization is resonantly coupled to a microwave cavity, leading to a superradiant burst in the microwave domain. b, Example of a delayed superradiant burst. A 1 mW pump is applied for 50 μs, after which a microwave superradiant burst is observed with a delay time τd. The superradiant signal is normalized by its peak-to-peak amplitude. c and d, Burst delay times, τd, and burst width, τw, measured as a function of the optical pump detuning, Δpump, which controls the optical transition strength from \(| g\rangle \) to \(| \uparrow \rangle \). A symmetric dependence of τd and τw is observed, with shorter delay times and narrower widths near resonance. This behaviour is consistent with the expected scaling τd, τw ∝ 1/N, as the pump detuning effectively controls the ensemble size, N, in the microwave spin manifold. Data points represent mean values, with error bars indicating the standard deviation over 300 repeated measurements.

a, Frequency-domain measurement of continuous-wave microwave superradiance, showing a much narrow linewidth of  ≈ 30 Hz. The inhomogeneously broadened ensemble line profile (dashed line) is overlaid for comparison. b, Dependence of the linewidth of continuous-wave superradiance on emission power, PMW. An inverse relationship between the linewidth and the emission power is observed, consistent with a noise-broadened Schawlow-Townes linewidth. The lower dashed line denotes the pump laser noise-limited bound. These results confirm that the disordered spin ensemble emits continuous-wave superradiance with a much narrower spectral linewidth. c, Continuous-wave superradiance emission frequency at different optical pump detunings. A linear correlation between the microwave emission frequency and optical pump detuning is observed, with a slope of  −1.23 kHz/MHz.

a, Four representative data traces under a 1 ms continuous optical pump. Random onset times of the emergent periodic pulsed phase are observed. b, Zoom-in of individual burst trains showing the distribution of burst onset times, {τk}, where k denotes the experimental repetition index. After an initial settling time, both the amplitudes, {Ak}, and the periodicity, T, become independent of k, indicating the establishment of a robust pulsed superradiance phase. c, Burst onset phases, defined as θk = 2π × τk/T (mod 2π), measured over 50 repetitions under identical experimental conditions. The phases are randomly distributed over 2π, demonstrating spontaneous breaking of continuous time-translation symmetry in the absence of any external timing reference.

a, Schematic of periodic pulsed superradiance, characterized by three parameters: the pulse-train periodicity T, the peak emission power Ppeak, and the average emission power \({\overline{P}}_{{\rm{MW}}}\). b-d, show fits to the experimental data presented in Fig. 3 of the main text, where T, Ppeak, and \({\overline{P}}_{{\rm{MW}}}\) exhibit good agreement with the expected scaling behaviours of T ∝ 1/N, Ppeak ∝ N2, and \({\overline{P}}_{{\rm{MW}}}\propto {N}^{2}\), respectively. Here, N is the effective number of spins in the microwave manifold, tuned via the optical pump detuning, Δpump. When sweeping Δpump, the optical pump power is fixed, corresponding to an excitation over an optical inhomogeneity Γop = 2π × 92 MHz in all three cases.

a, Relative contributions of superradiance (blue) and stimulated emission (red) to the emission strength in the periodic superradiance phase. b, Comparison of emission patterns between the many-body case with N = 1010 atoms (blue) and the single-atom case with N = 1 (red). For a fair comparison, the total effective cavity coupling strength is fixed to \({g}_{{\rm{tot}}}=\sqrt{N}g=2\pi \times 1\,{\rm{MHz}}\) for both cases. c, Comparison of emission patterns in the presence (blue) and absence (red) of spin frequency inhomogeneity, i.e., disorder. All simulations are performed using experimental parameters corresponding to the periodic superradiance phase in Regime III.

a and b, show simultaneously recorded microwave periodic superradiance and transferred optical periodic superradiance, respectively, over a duration of up to 100 ms. c, Zoom-in windows near 1, 50, and 100 ms showing synchronized dual-rail emission patterns, maintaining persistent and robust pulse periodicity without decay.

a, Microwave (blue) and optical (yellow) amplitudes, A(t), extracted from IQ detection as A(t) = ∣I(t) + iQ(t)∣. The I and Q signals, I(t) and Q(t), are measured continuously over 2 ms, capturing 30 consecutive superradiant bursts. The microwave and optical channels exhibit synchronized and reproducible temporal profiles. The grey shaded area indicates the noise floor determined from the optical signal, below which the phase extraction is not reliable. b, Normalized amplitude stability over 30 consecutive superradiant bursts. τ denotes the peak emission time, identified for each burst from the time-domain pulse train. The error bars denote the standard deviations of the microwave and optical normalized amplitudes, which are 0.009 and 0.05, respectively. c, Time-domain phase profiles, \(\phi (t)={\tan }^{-1}[Q(t)/I(t)]\), extracted from IQ detection. The microwave and optical pulse trains exhibit synchronized and reproducible phase profiles over time. Phase values in regions dominated by the optical-signal noise floor are greyed out, where large fluctuations are observed. The chirping behaviour during each pulse qualitatively follows the amplitude profile, which can be attributed to an effective Kerr nonlinearity induced intensity dependence. d, Phase stability over 30 consecutive superradiant bursts, zoomed in on the region above the noise floor. The error bars denote the standard deviations of the microwave and optical phase values, which are 0.03π and 0.11π, respectively. See Methods for details.

Cavity QED dynamics modelling and numerical simulation details, phase boundary estimation based on bifurcation and references.

#1292. Carrick weighs up stripping Bruno Fernandes of Man Utd captaincy

A defiant Michael Carrick refused to rule out stripping Bruno Fernandes of the captaincy as the Manchester United manager told his players to cut out their public sniping and start doing their talking on the pitch.

Carrick struck a bullish tone as he came out fighting and moved to reassert his authority after a tumultuous past fortnight that has left him battling to save his job ahead of Sunday’s must-win game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

The United manager began his press conference on Friday afternoon with a stirring five-and-a-half-minute monologue in which he issued an emotional call to arms to his players to demonstrate the values of hard work, sacrifice, humility and resilience that define the club.

Referencing Sir Matt Busby, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Bobby Charlton, Ryan Giggs and Wayne Rooney, Carrick warned there could be no “entitlement” culture in echoes of complaints from his predecessor Ruben Amorim.

United are actively considering their options in the event Carrick cannot quickly arrest a shocking start to the season that hit a new low with Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation by Como. The likes of Julian Nagelsmann, Eddie Howe, Unai Emery, Fabian Hürzeler and Antonio Conte are in the frame.

But Carrick insisted he was “100 per cent” convinced he was the right man to take United forward and, while he claimed the dressing room was “not divided”, he has had to contend with first defender Lisandro Martínez and then Fernandes venting in public.

Martínez was fined and publicly apologised for an extraordinary tirade at Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and the Old Trafford board last week before Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics in the wake of the Como debacle.

Carrick responded at the time to having his set-up and approach questioned by suggesting tactics count for little if players are unprepared to run.

Asked if he would consider taking the captaincy off Fernandes, Carrick said: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”

Pressed on whether Fernandes’s comments were all the more insidious and divisive at a time when the manager was trying to pull the squad together so soon after Martínez’s outburst, Carrick added: “Yeah, the most important thing for me is the team.

“First and foremost is the squad, the dynamics in the squad. And again, it’s about the club. And I’ll always do what’s best for the club.”

Carrick, Wilcox and United chief executive Omar Berrada held a meeting with Martínez in the wake of his criticism but the manager would not be drawn on whether he had spoken with Fernandes and it remains to be seen if he will be captain or start against Bournemouth.

“If I’ve spoken to him or haven’t spoken to him, I don’t think this is the time to go into too much detail,” he said.

Carrick agreed that United collectively needed to stop turning on each other in public. “We need to move forward in the right direction. We need to do things that enable us to do that. That’s pretty clear,” he said.

“It [the dressing room] is not divided, no. We just need to get back to doing what we do best and we will.”

Separately, Carrick expressed sympathy for Fernandes over the “awful” burglary at his home on Wednesday night when he was in Italy, and said the club “are doing a lot of work to support Bruno and his family”.

Carrick is under huge pressure heading into Bournemouth but said he was happy to take the heat if it enabled his players to perform.

“It is my responsibility whatever goes on the pitch, and what we are as a group, and what we look like, and what we feel like,” he said. “I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and for everyone else to stay dry.”

Nonetheless, Carrick admitted he was “hurting an awful lot” and that the team had to get back to showing the values and qualities that have underpinned the club’s historic success after a “really unacceptable” performance against Como and wider struggles. United have won two of 11 matches this season.

“I’m not entitled to be here,” Carrick said. “We’re not entitled to win. We’ve won in the past, we’ve got an incredible history, but that doesn’t mean you’re entitled to just win.

“I’m fully aware of that. It takes hard work, a lot of sacrifice. You’ve got to invest yourself in the club and you’ve got to do a lot of things that maybe aren’t so nice, but you’ve got to do it for each other, and you’ve got to win.

“It’s important we live up to that, and it’s important for me to push those values, and for our supporters to feel that moving forward.

“We’ve kind of lost our way a bit if I’m honest, and we will get it back. I’m totally confident we’ll get it back. Respect this club, respect what it takes, because it’s very important to me.”

Carrick added that he was inspired by the values of “humility, hard work, resilience, sacrifice and pride” embodied by the likes of Busby, Ferguson, Charlton, Giggs and Rooney.

“We can never lose that, and I won’t let us lose that,” he said. “We’ve had it for a spell, I feel very strongly about that. It inspires me a lot to live up to that and keep driving that with the players.

“There’s a resilience about this club that’s been shown for a long time. Whether that’s bouncing back from adversity, comebacks, late goals, success, sustaining success, there’s a resilience in this club that runs very deep.”

Carrick was trailed by a camera crew from Amazon Prime as he entered the media auditorium at Manchester United’s Carrington training base at 1.30pm on Friday.

There have been plenty of dark moments at Old Trafford in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era. But the difference this season is that any internal drama will soon be available for public consumption after the decision to allow cameras into a once-sacrosanct dressing room.

Whether Carrick will see out the next week, let alone a season being captured by filmmakers from Amazon’s All Or Nothing series, who probably cannot believe their luck at the unfolding crisis, remains to be seen. He certainly needs a big reaction against Bournemouth at Old Trafford at the very least.

But it became clear as he began his press conference with an emotional 5½-minute monologue that he would not go down without a fight.

🗣️ Commitment. Resilience. Teamwork. Michael's powerful message in full 👇 https://t.co/vWwJt1fW47

This was partly Carrick reasserting his own authority after a couple of weeks in which two senior players – defender Lisandro Martínez and captain Bruno Fernandes – decided to go public with their grievances and the team delivered a performance in the 4-1 hammering by Como that was up there with the very worst.

But a stony-faced Carrick was also sending a message to his squad to quit their public sniping and start pulling together for a wider cause. Moreover, to put the club and the team before yourself and your individual needs and complaints.

It was interesting that he used the word “entitlement”. His predecessor, Ruben Amorim, had uttered that same word to attack what he felt was an “entitlement culture” at the club and Carrick has evidently come to a similar conclusion.

"I think it's the feeling of entitlement that we have in our club" Ruben Amorim says some of the players at Manchester United may need a bit of a reality check 🎙️ https://t.co/PiJWML3TeH

In truth, so many of the post-Ferguson managers have spoken in similar ways – certainly Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Jose Mourinho and Ralf Rangnick.

Listening to Carrick repeatedly talking about the need for humility, hard work, pride, sacrifice and resilience was a reminder of how the values that were once taken for granted at this football club have steadily been eroded.

Wayne Rooney said this week that United’s players were “selfish” and “babies”. Many top players over the years have been selfish but it helped drive them and, in turn, their team to great heights, but the same cannot be said about the current bunch.

Carrick spoke about trying to rediscover something that is “lost” at the moment. Whether they can is a big if. Opponents aside, the only winners at the moment from United’s latest crisis are Amazon.

It feels at times as if it can be a long way away but it doesn’t take too much to flip the other way and we’re more than capable of doing that, I totally believe that.

We will. We’ll win football matches and we’ve got a very tough one on Sunday [against Bournemouth].

Very, very good team that we’re playing again and I’m not suggesting that becomes an easy game because it doesn’t. We’ve got to respect the game, respect what it takes to win.

We’ve spoken. There are always conversations going on. It’s pretty obvious how we’re all feeling. A reaction, a reaction from me.

The responsibility for me in this position is to lead. It is my responsibility, whatever goes on the pitch and what we look like, what we feel like.

Carrick had clearly thought hard about how he was going to tackle that today and what message he wanted to get across. The long and short of it was that the United manager was issuing a call to arms to his players to pull their finger out, respect the badge and start showing the kind of values of humility and hard work that the club is founded on. By name checking the likes of Sir Alex Ferguson and Matt Busby he was speaking about the people who exemplified the values United are all about

The foundations of this football club and values have been etched down for many years.

I totally understand and I get every single one of them. It comes down to being humble, to hard work and being really proud to live up to those values.

There is a resilience about this football club that has been shown for a long, long time. Whether that’s bouncing back from adversity, comebacks, late goals, sustaining success, there is a resilience to this football club that runs very, very deep.

No definitive answer from Carrick, who says he wants to do what is best for the football club.

There ends the broadcast section of the press conference after about 15 minutes.

Definitely a change in communication strategy from Carrick, speaking from the heart rather than waiting for questions.

My responsibility is to get a team on the pitch that represents this football club, represents the supporters and they can be proud of it with the identity that we show.

We have gone away from that just recently in certain games, which I’m fully aware of and definitely doing something about.

I think it’s important we all recognise that. I certainly recognise it. Our supporters of are the utmost importance to me and this football club.

For them to feel like they felt for five months at the start of the year and have that about us, that connection and that real vigour, intensity and enjoyment and passion is something we need to get back to.

Carrick says the dressing room is “not divided” but says it’s pretty clear the squad and everyone have to pull together and stop speaking out like has happened in public in response to questions about Martinez and Fernandes’ outbursts.

Principles are so important. We can win games, lose games, hopefully not but it can happen.

It’s how you do it and what it feels like is important for me. That the spirit and togetherness is there. It will be there. I’m working on solutions to move us forward.

I haven’t invented anything new, it’s the make-up of any good football team. You have to earn the right to be better than your opponent, that’s not changed and it never changes.

He says loads of conversations have been going on. He says it’s his responsibility “to lead” and that “I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and keep everyone else dry.”

Carrick adds on the Fernandes burglary. “It’s an awful thing to go through and we’re doing a lot of things to support him and his family.”

It was never about Ryan Giggs, it was never about Ryan Giggs, it was about Manchester United.

Wayne Rooney is top goalscorer of this football club. His biggest thing was playing for the team, sacrificing for the team and what was good for Manchester United.

Sir Alex Ferguson is the best manager of all-time. The greatest, for me. And working for him, his main priority was Manchester United.

Sir Matt [Busby] and Sir Bobby [Charlton], their resilience was beyond belief what they showed and how they rebuilt this football club. It was based on being humble, having humility and hard work. We can never lose that and I won’t let us lose that.

We’ve lost our way if I’m totally honest but we’ll get back what it takes.

Carrick has come in, trailed by the Amazon cameras, sat down and made an address for five minutes before taking any questions. He acknowledges it’s not been good enough or what the club expects and that it’s got to get better. He’s talking about rebuilding this club based on humility, values and hard work and won’t let that go and that it inspires him going forward. “Yeah we’re in a moment where it’s not going well but we need to show exactly what it means and respect what it means to be here and what it takes to win,” he said. “You’re not entitled to win. It takes hard work.”

I think it’s important... recently we haven’t had a good time I think that’s obvious, I totally accept that.

We had five months of relative success and I was happy with many things I was seeing.

We haven’t done well enough recently. Wednesday was a bad night for a lot of reasons, it really hurt a lot, it hurt me to see how the game panned out.

As I said after the game, it was unacceptable.

Hopefully he will be in position by half-past, but it is not unlike managers to keep everyone waiting.

My name has been linked with numerous clubs, but there are currently no negotiations at an advanced stage.

Following a wonderful and successful spell in charge of Napoli, I will take the time I need to consider how and when to return to management. It will be a carefully considered decision, one I will make when I believe the conditions are right.

I have read reports of financial demands and requests for full control that I have supposedly already made to the clubs mentioned, as well as reservations about what has been described as my “strong personality”. These reports are unfounded, as there is currently no concrete basis for such assessments.

Should a concrete opportunity arise, that will be the time to hold discussions with the club concerned and jointly consider the terms of a potential agreement, with due regard for both parties’ needs and the qualities and approach that define my work as a manager.

Until then, any assumptions about my demands and my professional future remain speculation and cannot be treated as fact.

For all his brilliance and ruthlessness as a businessman, Sir Jim Ratcliffe has yet to convince that he has any feel for football. Just look at the performance of Ineos’s other prize assets this season: Lausanne-Sport lie 12th in the 12-team Swiss top flight after one win in 10, and Nice are a distant 13th in Ligue 1, having burnt through eight different managers during the petrochemical giant’s seven years in charge.

As James Ducker and Sam Dean explore in this piece, a succession of Manchester United managers have admonished their team for a lack of industry and athleticism. A number of factors may be to blame: recruitment errors, paralysing pressure and a bad dressing-room culture among them. It is time to get back to basics.

Michael Carrick is not one of the Premier League’s more loquacious managers but supporters will be interested in what he has to say at his pre-Bournemouth press conference this afternoon.

The Manchester United manager is under severe pressure after a run of no wins in seven games across all competitions, and senior players are talking out of school in post-game interviews.

Just when it appeared a line had been drawn under Lisandro Martinez taking on technical director Jason Wilcox, Bruno Fernandes reached for a petrol can and poured more fuel on the flames.

Speaking after the dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como, Fernandes called out Carrick and his coaching staff for their tactical approach, specifically a reluctance to press opponents aggressively in a man-to-man fashion.

Carrick, by his own very measured standards, delivered a pointed response.

“We actually were half-pressed man to man in the second half and then conceded a goal from that,” he said. “And there’s a little bit on whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don’t run, and you don’t run forward, and you don’t run back, you ain’t going to win.”

Their opponents on Sunday are Bournemouth, who after a lean run of results under Marco Rose have just dispatched Sunderland for their first league victory of the season, and the mighty AC Milan in the Europa League.

Things do not get easier for United, who go to Stamford Bridge next weekend before a home game against Aston Villa before the November international break.

Telegraph Sport reported on Thursday that former Bayern Munich and Germany manager Julian Nagelsmann features prominently and is understood to want the job – as does Antonio Conte. United are also tracking Fabian Hurzeler while there is interest in Eddie Howe.

United are currently 13th in the table with seven points from seven games.

#1291. Ranking Every Premier League Manager by How Likely They Are to be Sacked

As the new Premier League season is now into its eleventh game week, it signifies that the resumption of the managerial merry-go-round is not far away from spinning again.

While some clubs sprang a surprise last term and seem to have their hierarchical structures firmly in place, the majority of clubs decided to go for something different, with as many as 50 per cent of the bosses in this season's division either managing a different club or being completely new to England's top flight.

And, in this results-driven business, the margin for error is razor-thin, with Ruben Amorim and Thomas Frank, who lost their respective positions at Manchester United and Tottenham last term, being the perfect examples of that.

Here, we explore the precarious world of Premier League management, assessing each manager's likelihood of facing the sack this season. From those navigating the treacherous waters of relegation battles to those leading title-chasing sides, we examine the factors that could impact managerial job security – from team performance trends and the patience of the boardroom to the constant glare of media attention.

Read on to find out which managers are sitting comfortably in their positions and which ones might need to keep a wary eye on the shadows of potential successors.

After finishing second in the Premier League for three seasons in a row, the Gunners finally ended a 22-year drought last season by winning gold. Silverware is the currency of success, but there's now a strong feeling that Mikel Arteta has the tools at his disposal to keep pushing on for even dizzier heights after coming oh-so close to success in the Champions League and League Cup, too.

The hierarchy knows full well that they have a manager capable of turning one success into a dynasty. Funds were there, it seemed, to pluck Vinicius Jr from Real Madrid, showing how ambitious the club are even if a deal could be done. There's no question that Arsenal are favourites for back-to-back titles, and a new contract in October 2026 only cements his position further.

The inevitable happened during November's international break when Manchester United sacked Michael Carrick after four defeats and one win in 10 league games. The under-pressure INEOS turned to Mauricio Pochettino, paying his release clause to lure him away from the United States national team job.

Pochettino is perhaps the biggest name to take the reins at Old Trafford since Jose Mourinho in 2016 and the Argentine is given a massive mountain to climb. As things stand, United are 19th heading into December and his first job is to ensure they escape the relegation zone.

Given the situation, the onus is less on Pochettino to deliver immediate trophy success and more on turning the tide. He'll likely be judged in the coming months, but a two-and-a-half-year contract doesn't exactly fill fans with confidence.

Replacing Roberto De Zerbi was no mean feat, but the arrival of former St Pauli boss Fabian Hurzeler has seemingly proven why many think Brighton owner Tony Bloom is one of the best business-minded custodians in the beautiful game. He's unearthed one of the most exciting tacticians in Europe in Hurzeler.

GIVEMESPORT Key Statistic: Fabian Hurzeler is the youngest permanent manager in Premier League history, as he became the head coach of Brighton & Hove Albion at the age of 31 years and 173 days two summers back.

In February 2025, their humiliating 7-0 loss to Nottingham Forest could have caused turmoil at the Amex, but Texas-born Hurzeler and his side put it behind them and showed real character to maintain steady, if not particularly amazing, league form to finish eighth for the second season in a row. The Seagulls have started 2026/27 very well, and look set to challenge for European football once again, as their masterclass in goalscoring means they could even be considered among the title challengers.

If there's any team in world football that stands by the ethos that managers need time, it's Liverpool. In many cases, Anfield's helmsman is revered, cherished, and held in higher regard than the players. It's a rare club tradition, but one that stretches as far back as the pre-Shankly years, with Jurgen Klopp's tenure the perfect encapsulation of such a notion.

Jurgen Klopp, Pep Guardiola and Sir Alex Ferguson boast some of the best points-per-match averages in Premier League history.

Because of this, Andoni Iraola should be feeling pretty cosy for a while on Merseyside. He will receive the full backing of FSG and his new supporters, unless his values go down the drain like his predecessor, Arne Slot. It would seem Anfield's residents would love a personality and playing style of Klopp's stature, and the Spaniard might fulfil that desire well, having lost just twice in the league so far.

Marco Rose is a good, tactically astute manager, particularly known for his high-pressing, modern, and attacking style of football - something Bournemouth's squad is already geared towards. The only thing he currently lacks is Premier League experience, which raised a few eyebrows upon his appointment.

He has big boots to fill in Andoni Iraola's void, but a board with very little expectation - and the fact he has a good track record of managing sides in Europe - means he should get more than enough time to show the rest of the league what he's all about. And after a worrying start, his Cherries are now growing, with nine wins in a row across competitions and up to fourth in the table.

When there is talk and murmurs of your owners looking at potential replacements after you achieve promotion to the Premier League, you know you're in for a bumpy ride. That's the situation Daniel Farke found himself in after guiding Leeds United to the Championship title in the 2024-25 season.

Farke was feeling the heat in April, despite his Peacocks side having already sealed promotion at the time. The German perhaps wasn't the Hollywood name the 49ers wanted at the helm, with shock links to three-time Premier League title-winner Jose Mourinho emerging. But there was no managerial change, and the 50-year-old was handed the chance to prove he's the right man for the job.

So far, so good. After all, beating Forest 1-0 away from home in his opening game of the new campaign is the perfect way to begin proving that second-season syndrome is just a myth. And perhaps the best result of his time at Elland Road came in late November with a famous 4-1 win away to Chelsea at Stamford Bridge.

A manager with a point to prove, Thomas Frank returned to Premier League management with Crystal Palace after replacing Pierre Sage in late November. After a nightmare spell at Tottenham, the Dane will be hoping to get his reputation back on track at Selhurst Park.

The former Brentford boss got off to the worst possible start, losing 3-2 away to fellow relegation battlers Coventry City. It's still very early to assess Frank and whether he'll be a success in South London, but he's taken over a side that looks a polar opposite to the UEFA Conference League-winning team of 2025-26.

Brentford fans were dreading the day Thomas Frank decided to move on, and that came last summer as he decided to replace Ange Postecoglou at Tottenham Hotspur. Replacing the Dane was always going to be a tough task for the Bees' higher-ups and their bold appointment of Keith Andrews raised eyebrows.

Andrews was a member of Frank's backroom team, working as the team's set-piece coach and gaining valuable experience for a first-team management role. The Irishman hasn't had to work his way through the footballing pyramid as he's been thrown into a Premier League job from the off. Risky, indeed, but he's settled in extremely well.

He led the club to a ninth-placed finish in his debut season as a Premier League manager and his side have lost just twice in 10 matches to start the 26/27 campaign. His job is as secure as any in England right now as his side sit firmly in the top 10.

The former Arsenal coach didn't enjoy a great time in England while in north London but has managed to rejuvenate his Premier League reputation with a fantastic spell at Aston Villa so far.

Indeed, Unai Emery has taken the Villans back into Europe – where he has a formidable record – and built an exciting team. With the likes of Ollie Watkins and Morgan Rogers darting about in attack, he won yet another Europa League title last time out.

The addition of midweek Champions League football could prove a challenge for Emery's squad, but their taste of the big time has made his troops lust for more. The acquisition of World Cup star Johan Manzambi should ease squad depth concerns, and Emery's longevity means he has plenty of brownie points to bank, despite a slow start – just like last term – which saw them pick up just two wins from their opening seven league games before roaring back into their best form with wins over Newcastle and Man City.

The times were a-changing at Everton following the return of David Moyes a little over a season ago, as he made an immediate impact after replacing Sean Dyche in January 2025. His poorly performing Toffees side were in the midst of yet another relegation battle after being hit with a 10-point deduction for Financial Fair Play breaches.

The Merseyside Blues are right back on track under Moyes' watch, though, with The Freidkin Group setting them up nicely before then announcing their plans to sell the club already. James Tarkowski suggested that they were aiming for Europe, and you wouldn't put it past Moyes fulfilling that ambition, even if last season saw their form dip during the second half of the campaign.

A 2-0 home win over Crystal Palace and draws against Bournemouth, Tottenham and Man United to kick off was a strong way to start 2026/27.

Been there as a fan—staying up late hoping for a spark after a rough night. Hang in there, Howe; football breaks our hearts, then somehow we come back for more drama.

#1290. D’Amico: ‘Roma want to reinforce in January, not sell Kone’

Roma director Tony D’Amico assures Manu Koné is not leaving in January, as the ‘aim is to reinforce the squad’ mid-season, and explains some of the squad rotation against Parma.

It kicks off at the Stadio Tardini at 17.00 GMT (18.00 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from today’s four Serie A games on the Liveblog.

The injury crisis is finally starting to calm down for the Giallorossi, as only Devyne Rensch and Lorenzo Pellegrini failed to make the trip to Parma this evening.

Mile Svilar had not played in over two months after fracturing a finger in training, while Paulo Dybala also had not featured since October 14, but they both start today.

Wesley and Matias Soulé are among those rested today, ahead of the upcoming Champions League clash with Paris Saint-Germain.

“The break for international duty always has a certain sense of unknown quantity, but the coach chose the players who remained here, we have some from Argentina and Brazil who only arrived late, but we are confident that we’ll have a good game,” D’Amico told DAZN Italia.

The January transfer window is coming up, so is there a specific budget or list of options drawn up, like Endrick of Real Madrid and Ademola Lookman with Atletico Madrid, who of course worked with Gian Piero Gasperini at Atalanta.

Specifically, D’Amico was asked about the rumours that France international Koné will be targeted by big clubs again after a difficult summer.

“It is premature to talk about this now, as there are many variables that can change from now to January. The aim is to reinforce the squad, and therefore anyone asking about Kone leaving, that is not strengthening the team.

“We discuss the situation with the coach every day, the characteristics of players we imagine can give something extra to the side. The January window is one based on opportunities, so we’ll have to see what happens.”

Roma went into the break for international duty just two points off Serie A leaders Lazio, as they aim to improve on last season’s third-place finish.

“It is not just about technical quality, but temperamental and mental strength too. We believe in the whole squad, and that also means testing those who need a chance to prove they can step up when required,” concluded D’Amico.

#1289. ‘I Made Millions Alongside Lionel Messi - But I Was Happier Earning €113 in Prison’

It's a dream of any footballer to be able to make millions and play alongside Lionel Messi but one of his former teammates preferred prison and earning far less.

Footballers don't usually swap winning trophies at the most famous stadiums around the world for incarceration as the fame that comes with the profession should prevent them from criminality. Some, unfortunately, can't help themselves and not even their riches or celebrity status are enough.

There are many high-profile football names who have landed in prison after their playing careers, including the disgraced Robinho and Joey Barton. Those two remain behind bars, unlike Dani Alves who, after spending 839 days in prison, was acquitted on appeal and had his charges overturned.

In January 2023, former Barcelona full-back Alves was arrested and accused of sexually assaulting a young woman in a Barcelona nightclub in December 2022. Handed a four and a half year prison sentence in February 2024, his provisional release came in March of that year after he paid €1 million in bail.

Alves became a free man in March 2025 when the top court in the Spanish region of Catalonia overturned his conviction. It ruled that the earlier verdict contained a number of inconsistencies and that the evidence presented was insufficient to overcome the presumption of innocence.

The 43-year-old's lengthy stay in prison came after a successful football career, becoming one of the most decorated players in history. A former 126-cap Brazil international, he won titles with club and country, including three Champions League trophies with Messi and Luis Suarez at Barcelona.

That period of Alves' career should be the best days of his life, but instead he values his time in incarceration more. That's because the Brazilian turned to faith while serving time.

Alves has now become an evangelical preacher and holds religious talks, of which, during his latest he reflected on his time in Brians 2 prison. He explained why he preferred the small amount of money gained from working while in prison to that of the millions that came while winning at Camp Nou:

"I was earning millions of euros, thank God, but in prison, earning 113 euros, I was happier than I was when I was earning millions."

Alves spoke of his relationship with God and how he asks a lot of questions, describing himself as a 'child before Him'. This spiritual transformation he has gone through has given him a new outlook on life and that money isn't as important as he once felt during his playing career.

The 29-year-old represented Manchester City at youth level, as well as Wolves and Nottingham Forest at senior level.

Away from religious speaking, Alves does remain tied to the sport, currently holding a co-ownership stake in Portuguese club Sao Jao de Ver. He retired from the game after arrest in January 2023, having won 46 trophies.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#1288. Revealed: Tottenham's aggressive youth recruitment campaign to snap up Britain's best teenage stars and blow rivals out of the water - with the help of expensive private schools and lucrative pro deals

Published: 07:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 07:00 EST, 20 November 2026

Tottenham Hotspur have launched an aggressive campaign to recruit Britain's most talented young footballers from rivals, using expensive private education and lucrative professional contracts to lure them in.

Daily Mail Sport can reveal Spurs are targeting the country's most talented Under 15s through a bespoke package, headed by hefty wages when youngsters turn professional aged 17 and free education at one of the country's finest private schools.

And a glimpse of what the future might look like came against Crystal Palace on October 31.

With Tottenham 2-0 up, Roberto De Zerbi introduced 18-year-old academy graduate Luca Williams-Barnett in the 88th minute. The eye-catching cameo proved a memorable Premier League debut, and last week earned him the top flight's Creative Moment of the Month award for a mazy dribble through Palace's defence.

It's further evidence of the talent coming through at Spurs. Williams-Barnett is not a product of the new recruitment drive, but he offers an illustration of what the club hope to achieve by nurturing talented youngsters and giving them opportunities in the first team.

That has not always been Tottenham's strength, having endured a decade of failing to turn potential into established first-team players. Since Harry Kane and Andros Townsend made their league debuts in 2012, only three Spurs academy graduates – Ryan Mason, Harry Winks and Oliver Skipp – have made at least 30 Premier League appearances for the club.

A glimpse of what Tottenham's future might look like came against Crystal Palace on October 31 with Luca Williams-Barnett's thrilling cameo off the bench

Since Harry Kane and Andros Townsend (left) made their debuts, only Harry Winks, Ryan Mason (right) and Oliver Skipp have made 30 top-flight appearances from Spurs' academy

In a Daily Mail Sport interview last month, ex-Spurs player and manager Tim Sherwood claimed Tottenham's inability to give youngsters a proper pathway to the first team has failed those in the set-up over the past decade, and that the academy may as well be 'closed up'.

It is a record the club are determined to change. Spurs' renewed strategy has been felt across the Premier League's academy circuit over the past year, with rivals anxious at what lies ahead.

The competition for young players is growing. As well as the traditional Big Six clubs, Newcastle, Aston Villa and Brighton have also become worthy competitors because of the first-team pathways they offer.

Tottenham pay £21,000-a-year fees to St John's Senior School in Enfield, which boasts top grades and facilities. Its most recent GCSE cohort achieved 65.3 per cent grades 9–7, formerly known as A* and A grades. The school's football pitch has 22 water cannons underneath (the same number as Arsenal's Emirates Stadium) and both primary and secondary drainage systems.

The programme presented to the parents of prospective stars is the key selling point. Spurs have been given permission by the league to provide a Full-Time Training Module (FTTM) programme which allows students more time away from school. They have their lessons at St John's but on three days a week after lunch, they go to the training ground and focus on football. It is the school's responsibility to organise catch-up lessons so education is not missed out on.

Arsenal, Manchester City, Brighton and Wolves were the first adopters of FTTM, and now Spurs have joined them. Where Tottenham have elevated their strategy is in the number of schoolboys whose fees they cover. Daily Mail Sport understands Spurs have awarded multiple FTTMs to pupils, covering fees in excess of £300,000 annually.

Through this, the club have been able to lure in some of the country's best talents. Isaac Allen, who has captained the England Under 15s, joined Spurs from West Ham in August despite Arsenal's attempts to sign him. The 15-year-old struck four goals in three matches at the Under-15 World Cup last month. Gabriel Rigg, 15, was also recruited from West Ham in September, while Spurs beat Arsenal, Chelsea and Newcastle to the signing of Jake Maloney, 14, from Charlton.

The most promising among the cohort is Ashiah Haughton-Sinclair, who in September trained with Spurs' first team. Last season the 15-year-old became the youngest player to feature for their Under 18s, and netted 70 goals and 20 assists.

Troy Parrott (right) came through the youth set-up but struggled for game time behind Kane. He left for AZ Alkmaar in 2024, and this summer signed for Real Betis

Marcus Edwards (right) is another Spurs academy product who made the grade elsewhere, scoring at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium for Sporting Lisbon in 2022

Spurs' Hotspur Way base, opened in 2012, is renowned as being one of the finest training complexes in European football, and is regularly used by the England team

Tottenham's ambitions didn't stop there, as they tried to recruit other players from rivals last summer. The club thought Kyran Thompson was joining from Arsenal, before Newcastle snapped up the talented forward at the last minute. Mishel Nduka, also previously at Arsenal, was approached by Tottenham before he chose a lucrative deal at Manchester City.

Daily Mail Sport understands Spurs pay higher salaries than most Premier League clubs – bar Man City and Chelsea – for academy stars signing professional terms aged 17, which is the earliest age allowed.

This is a significant bargaining chip, as many clubs are rigid in what they will offer players signing their first professional contract.

There is typically the belief that too much, too young can have a negative impact, but Spurs view it as a necessary ingredient in the modern competition for talent. Nurturing academy graduates into the first team negates the need to spend millions later down the line on established players.

The Tottenham aim is for their first team in the next five years to be reinforced by multiple leading academy graduates, after a decade of producing promising talent – such as Marcus Edwards and Troy Parrott, now at Burnley and Real Betis respectively – without giving them a viable pathway at the club.

And those surplus to requirements could be sold for substantial fees. Luka Vuskovic (£50million to Brighton), Will Lankshear (£20m to Middlesbrough), Ashley Phillips (£20m to Middlesbrough) and Alfie Devine (£6m to Preston North End) are recent examples.

Facilities play a part, too. Spurs' Hotspur Way base, opened in 2012, is renowned as one of the finest training complexes in European football.

The 77-acre state-of-the-art complex in Enfield, which cost £45m to build in 2012 and has since seen significant investment, is home to both the first team and academy, as well as being used regularly by England.

Luka Vuskovic was snapped up before his price tag got too high, and then was sold to Brighton for £50million this summer when he couldn't break into the starting line-up

Will Lankshear earned Spurs another £20m when he left for Middlesbrough

With Williams-Barnett already offering a glimpse of what lies ahead, Spurs will hope he is the first of many academy graduates to make the leap

While four of the 15 grass pitches are reserved exclusively for first-team training, the youngsters benefit from being immersed in the same elite environment as the senior professionals they aspire to emulate. It's an arrangement designed to make the pathway from youth prospect to Premier League footballer feel that little bit closer.

With Williams-Barnett already offering a glimpse of what lies ahead, Spurs will hope he is the first of many academy graduates to make the leap, rather than another reminder of the potential they have previously allowed to slip through their fingers.

For a club that has spent the best part of a decade searching for its next homegrown star, the teenager could yet become the face of a long-overdue academy revival.

#1287. Gattuso: ‘So proud of Lazio mentality, we play at high tempo’

Gennaro Gattuso expressed his ‘pride’ as Lazio swept Lecce aside 3-0 to stay top of the Serie A table. ‘I don’t mind misplaced passes, because we play at such a high tempo.’

The Aquile will spend at least another week on top of the Serie A table following today’s 3-0 victory over Cagliari at the Stadio Olimpico.

Tijjani Noslin found the net twice before Davide Frattesi put the cherry on top with a delightful lob in the final minutes of the match.

“I am proud of the mentality and the hunger shown by the team today,” Gattuso told DAZN Italia.

“We didn’t have the best start, but then got control of the game, both in possession and off the ball. Lecce are an uncomfortable opponent, they always come and push you, so it is fundamental for us to keep this attitude.”

There is always some concern for coaches after the break for international duty, but Gattuso assures he had no such qualms about his Lazio players.

“I saw the way they were training, so I was not worried. There is a great spirit and application, we’ve got to keep going like this. It is all down to the players, they are putting in the right mentality, hunger and sense of belonging. They are doing something incredible.”

Lazio are top of the table and still unbeaten in Serie A despite a lot of injury problems, as today they were missing Mattia Zaccagni, Nuno Tavares, Josip Sutalo and Adam Marusic.

Nicolò Rovella also came off the bench late on and is still trying to work his way back to full fitness after numerous issues.

“Rovella can give us more vertical passes, as when he gets the ball, he immediately looks up and forward,” explained the coach.

“I think we also need to talk about Fisayo Dele-Bashiru. He deserves more. We’ve got to give Rovella playing time so that he can regain fitness, then he can give us an important hand.”

Considering how well Lazio are doing under Gattuso so far this season, is there anything he still hasn’t seen and wants them to improve?

“I don’t mind losing the ball with misplaced passes that much, because when you play at a high tempo, that can happen. I am more interested in the mentality of the side and how they are hanging in there under pressure.

“I am satisfied, you always want something more, but at this tempo there are going to be some misplaced passes. We can improve our reading of the game, as for example today when we struggled to get through the middle, we needed to spread the game out wide.”

#1286. Widespread deciduousness reveals diverse Amazonian phenological strategies

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The Amazon rainforest is a cornerstone of regional and global carbon cycling1 and is widely regarded and modelled as a perennially evergreen ecosystem2,3. This prevailing view, however, masks substantial fine-scale variation in leaf phenology, limiting our capacity to predict ecosystem responses to climate change. Here by combining 10-m Sentinel-2 observations with machine learning, we uncover pervasive, spatially structured seasonal deciduousness across the basin. In 70.0% of the Amazon, leaf shedding precedes leaf flushing by at least 3 months, creating pronounced asynchrony between deciduousness and greenness seasonality, whereas the remainder shows near-synchronous phenology. Hydroclimate emerges as the dominant factor associated with this asynchrony across 51.6% of the area, followed by soil properties (33.2%) and light availability (15.2%). Motivated by this widespread decoupling between deciduousness and canopy greenness, we incorporated deciduousness-constrained leaf turnover and the resulting leaf-age demography into ecophysiological models, yielding spatially widespread improvements in the seasonal agreement between simulated gross primary productivity and satellite-derived photosynthetic seasonality across 79.9% of the basin. These findings challenge the conventional view of Amazonian phenology, demonstrating that previously overlooked deciduousness influences Amazonian carbon dynamics. Incorporating these insights into process-based models is essential for refining projections of climate–forest feedbacks in the Amazon and for understanding its ecological functions under accelerating global change.
