Site information, including location, data type, and observation period, is provided in Supplementary Table 1. The map was created using ArcGIS Pro with the Esri World Ocean Base basemap. Basemap sources: Esri, Garmin, GEBCO, NOAA NGDC and other contributors.

Panels a-e compare the temporal dynamics of ecosystem-scale deciduousness fraction from Sentinel-2 (blue line) with the fraction of leafless tree crowns visually assessed from phenocam images (black line). The Sentinel-2 deciduousness fraction is calculated as the mean value within a 500 m × 500 m area centred on each phenocam site, while the phenocam typically covers an area of approximately 100 m × 100 m. Panel f shows the relationship between Sentinel-2-derived deciduousness and the corresponding deciduousness derived from phenocam observations across five sites (n = 60 paired site-month observations). The solid line indicates an ordinary least-squares linear regression, with statistical significance assessed using a two-sided test (p = 6.17 × 10−22).

a, Relationship between standardized monthly litterfall and standardized satellite-derived deciduousness across annual cycles at 47 Amazonian sites (n = 559 pooled site-month observations). The red line indicates the ordinary least-squares linear regression across all pooled data, and the inset boxplot summarizes the site-level distribution of correlation coefficients (r, n = 47 sites). b, Relationship between satellite-derived deciduousness amplitude and the ground-derived proportion of deciduous tree species across the Amazon basin. Grey circles represent raw plot-to-pixel observations (n = 289 plots). The red line shows the ordinary least-squares linear fit to the raw observations, and the shaded band indicates the 95% confidence interval of the fitted mean relationship. The dashed grey line indicates the 1:1 relationship. For a and b, statistical significance of the regression slopes was assessed using two-sided tests (a, p = 2.52 × 10−141; b, p = 7.24 × 10−28). The p values were not adjusted for multiple comparisons. c, Patch-level comparison of deciduousness derived from Sentinel-2 (y-axis) against that derived from closely date-matched, high-resolution Google Earth imagery (GEI; x-axis) via image-specific Random Forest classification and pooled across all 16 validation scenes. Each dot represents a 100-m × 100-m aggregated patch (n = 6058 patches), and the dashed black line marks the 1:1 relationship. d, e, Scene-level distributions of correlation coefficients (r; d) and root-mean-square errors (RMSE; e) calculated separately for each of the 16 GEI validation scenes. Grey dots represent individual scenes. In all boxplots, the centre line indicates the median, the box bounds the interquartile range (IQR), and the whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR.

a, c, e, g, Spatial maps of evergreen forest cover (a), MODIS Vegetation Continuous Fields tree cover (c), EVI amplitude (e) and VOD amplitude (g). Inset histograms show the basin-wide frequency distribution of each metric. b, d, f, h, Corresponding pixel-level relationships between Sentinel-2-derived deciduousness amplitude and the four reference metrics. Hexbin colour indicates observation density, and dashed lines indicate least-squares linear regressions. Sample sizes (b, d, f, h) were n = 227,612, 227,612, 226,942 and 221,884 valid paired forest pixels, reflecting product-specific data availability. All two-sided tests gave p < 10−300. Correlation coefficients (r) and regression equations are shown in each panel.

Panels a-h show how each variable affects deciduousness–greenness asynchrony, with positive SHAP values (>0) indicating a positive effect and negative SHAP values (<0) indicating a negative effect. The black line in each panel represents a fitted line, summarizing the central tendency of the data points.

Bar charts show the proportional influence of hydroclimate, soil, and light for the entire basin (a), Southern Amazon (b), Guiana Shield (c), and Everwet Amazon (d).

a-c, Spatial patterns of model-performance gain, expressed as the change in the correlation coefficient (Δr) between the GPP seasonality simulated by LD-LUE and that simulated by each corresponding conventional LUE model, with both evaluated against satellite SIF. Results are shown for the EC-LUE (a), two-leaf EC-LUE (TL-EC-LUE; b) and MODIS-LUE (c). Positive Δr indicates better agreement of LD-LUE with satellite SIF relative to its conventional counterpart. Insets show the basin-wide distributions of Δr, with the red dashed line marking Δr = 0 and the annotated values indicating the percentage of forest pixels with Δr > 0.

a-l, Comparisons of monthly GPP seasonality at four Amazonian EC flux-tower sites (K34, K67, CAX, and RJA). Rows correspond to the three core LUE formulations: EC-LUE (a-d), TL-EC-LUE (e-h), and MODIS-LUE (i–l). Black dashed lines with open circles represent EC observations. Coloured lines with open markers represent conventional baselines driven by various vegetation inputs (e.g., NDVI, EVI, kNDVI, MODIS-LAI), whereas solid red lines with filled markers denote the LD-LUE models. m, n, Dumbbell plots showing site-level performance and across-site mean in terms of the temporal correlation coefficient (r) (m) and RMSE (n). Open symbols denote the conventional baselines, whereas the corresponding filled symbols denote the LD-LUE models. The vertical lines connecting each pair indicate the magnitude and direction of performance changes following incorporation of the LD module. Symbol colours distinguish the baseline input configurations, and symbol shapes indicate the underlying model formulations (circles, EC-LUE; triangles, TL-EC-LUE; squares, MODIS-LUE).

a-d, Spatial distribution of model performance gain, expressed as Δr, for EC-LUE (a), TL-EC-LUE (b), MODIS-LUE (c), and mean Δr across the three models (d). Δr is calculated as the difference in the correlation coefficient between satellite SIF and the GPP seasonality simulated by the LD-LUE model (that incorporates both satellite deciduousness-constrained structural inputs and leaf demography) and that simulated by the corresponding baseline model (which includes only satellite deciduousness-constrained structural inputs). Positive values indicate improved seasonal agreement with SIF after incorporating leaf-age-dependent physiological dynamics, whereas negative values indicate reduced agreement. Insets show the basin-wide distributions of Δr, with the red dashed line marking Δr = 0 and the annotated values indicating the percentage of forest pixels with Δr > 0. e, Stacked bar chart showing the proportional breakdown of pixels with improved (red) and degraded (blue) Δr averaged across the three models, for each ecoregion (Southern Amazon, Guiana Shield, and Everwet Amazon) and the entire Amazon basin.

a-d, Comparison of monthly GPP seasonality at four Amazonian EC flux-tower sites: K34 (a), K67 (b), CAX (c), and RJA (d). Red lines with triangles represent the full leaf-demography-enabled model (LD-LUE), while blue lines with squares represent the baseline model (LAIdec-LUE), which uses the same deciduousness-derived LAI but assumes a seasonally fixed photosynthetic capacity. Black dashed lines with open circles indicate the EC-derived GPP observations. Shaded bands indicate ±1 standard error of the mean (SEM; n = 3 LUE formulations per ensemble). e-g, Quantitative assessment of model performance gains across the four sites, comparing LD-LUE (red bars) and LAIdec-LUE (blue bars) in terms of correlation coefficient (r; e), root mean square error (RMSE; f), and amplitude ratio (g). The amplitude ratio in (g) is calculated relative to the observed seasonal amplitude, with the horizontal dashed line at 1.0 indicating perfect agreement.

#1285. Milan owner Cardinale on Endrick: ‘One of the best players in the world in his position’

Gerry Cardinale has described Endrick as one of the best players in the world in his position, although he insists Milan’s project is bigger than any one player.

Speaking to MilanNews.it ahead of Sunday’s game against Frosinone at San Siro, the Rossoneri owner confirmed Milan will spend in January, but only on signings that fit the club’s plans.

“We’re ready. We’re doing a lot of work. As we discussed, it’s complicated, and the January transfer market is always tricky, so you have to be prepared and opportunistic,” Cardinale said. “One thing I can admit is that we’re not making any decisions we don’t feel great about. We’re going to spend money, but we’re going to spend it smartly, consistent with the project and in close coordination with Ruben and the guys here at Milanello.”

Milan have been strongly linked with Endrick, with reports suggesting they’re ready to meet Real Madrid’s €60m valuation, but Club Brugge’s Nicolò Tresoldi is also being considered as an alternative.

“Look, that name is also mentioned a lot. This project is more than just one player,” Cardinale said. “He is one of the best players, if not the best player, in the world in his position. I have a tremendous amount of respect for him. We’ll see what’s possible in the market.”

Cardinale wouldn’t confirm Markus Krösche’s arrival as head of football. Corriere dello Sport has reported that the Eintracht Frankfurt director will start on 1 January.

“You guys are very focused on Markus Krösche. That name has been bandied about. When we’re ready to make an announcement, I’ll come back to you on that.”

He also spoke warmly about Adrien Rabiot, who is in talks over a new contract.

“I love Adrien, he’s one of my favourite players. I think he’s fantastic, and I have a tremendous amount of respect for him and his family. We’re in discussions and I hope we’ll get a good result. If it were up to me, he’d be a franchise player for this team.”

Fourth-placed Milan face sixth-placed Frosinone on Sunday at 18:00 CET [17:00 GMT].

“We’ve had a great couple of days and great sessions at Casa Milan on the January market, and on all our plans for the rest of this season and into next summer,” Cardinale added. “The mood here is really upbeat. We had a great practice today, and the team is really coming together. I spoke to a lot of the players, and they understand, as Ruben said, how important this game is. Hopefully we come out strong and get the win.”

If you mean as a non playing substitute one the best in the world or the best sure, why not!

If mean it literally it’s laughable, he’s nowhere near one of the best in his position, and definitely not the best – on what grounds? Can’t start for Madrid, barely a sub. If that good he would be starting, nonsense chat. Do Milan need Endrick? Inflated hype and price as he’s from Brazil and Madrid (yet done zero for either). His wonderkid tag has gone now, he’s 20.

#1284. Fabregas on Jacobo Ramón: ‘He arrives in the box with more aggression than a striker’

Cesc Fabregas praised Jacobo Ramón’s attacking threat after the defender scored in Como’s 2-0 win over Cagliari, although he insisted the performance was far from perfect.

With quotes via TuttoMercatoWeb, Ramón headed Como in front from Yan Couto’s assist in the 24th minute, and Lucas Da Cunha added a second, also set up by Couto, early in the second half. The win takes Fabregas’ side up to fourth for now, and Como remain unbeaten at the Sinigaglia in Serie A this season.

“Perfect? No. We conceded four counter-attacks, three of them big chances where they could have scored,” Fabregas said. “They did something different going forward and found space in behind us, but from around the 35th minute things changed, and in the second half there was only one team on the pitch.

“I’m very happy for the lads. There was so much energy, and Lahdo came on very well. We had to finish with two right-backs because we don’t have the players. Today my only attacking option on the bench was Nico Paz.”

Ramón has just been called up by Spain for the first time, and Fabregas believes his scoring has improved a lot.

“There are players who are stronger, but he’s a player I like. I won’t say too much about how I feel about him, because he might read it later,” Fabregas joked. “We worked a lot on his finishing. Last year he couldn’t score in front of goal, even easy chances. Now he scores them. It shows you they’re kids, but they improve every year.

“He arrives in the box with more aggression than a striker, even when you don’t expect it, and he can play long and short. In the air, he’s first or second in Serie A for duels won. But if you want to reach the top, you have to handle Thuram and Esposito, so the lads understand they always have to do more to get to that level.

“In five or six years, I’d like to see all these lads playing at World Cups and winning the Champions League. They have the chance to grow here.”

Da Cunha started despite his efforts with France this week, because Maxence Caqueret picked up a minor problem on Friday.

“Honestly, I wanted to rest him today, but we can’t take risks now, we’re down to 11, 12, 13 players. He’s a gem for us. He always raises the level. I’d like every player in the world to have Da Cunha’s mentality.”

He also warned there’s no room to ease off.

“There are seven games left before Christmas, and everyone has to play their part.”

#1283. ‘Tactical genius’ Emery outsmarts Maresca as City crash to first league defeat

Enzo Maresca’s flawless start to the Premier League with Manchester City is over after another masterclass from Unai Emery.

Matches at Villa Park were a notoriously chastening experience for Pep Guardiola and it was the same old story for Maresca as City have now lost on their last four visits here.

On his fourth anniversary in charge of Villa, there was more tactical brilliance from Emery, who also did the double over Guardiola last season. It was Emery’s £65m record signing Nicolas Jackson who again underlined how some managers can get the best out of certain players.

Jackson had been a target for Emery ever since the Basque’s appointment and now has seven goals in claret and blue. It will have been an especially sweet moment for the Senegal forward, for it was Maresca who allowed him to join Bayern Munich on loan while he was in charge at Chelsea.

City’s run of seven league wins in a row always looked in danger here against a vibrant and energetic Villa. Maresca will also reflect on two poor goals conceded after errors from Marc Guéhi and goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma.

Guéhi endured a particularly difficult afternoon and was at fault for Jackson’s stunning first goal. The centre-back has struggled in recent weeks with a bad mistake in England’s defeat by Spain and he was exposed for both Ipswich goals last week. He was replaced at half-time after a booking for a foul on the excellent Jackson.

What a strike from Nicolas Jackson to beat Gianluigi Donnarumma 😲 Villa Park erupts 🔊 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/zkuDVMevKF

Maresca said: “I’m not worried about Marc at all, he is playing every game since the season started for us and the national team so it’s not easy. He is ok, it [taking him off] was just a technical decision and like in all games managers make changes. He was on a yellow card and sometimes one yellow card can be dangerous.”

When asked if the goals were avoidable, Maresca said: “Absolutely, both. Sometimes you have to be a bit more lucky because we only conceded those two chances. We will try again to win at Villa next season. I don’t think we deserved to lose but we learn from that and move on. You can always learn something. For sure there are things we can do better today.”

While much of the focus will be on City’s 100 per cent start to the league coming to an end, Emery got everything right here. From his team selection to his set-up and substitutions, he outsmarted Maresca on many levels. After the game, Villa defender Matty Cash described his manager as “a tactical genius”.

It was four years ago to the day that Emery grabbed this famous club by the shirt and collar and gave them an almighty shake. After a summer of much instability including many player sales, he appears to have already struck a formula with his newly assembled team.

There were a number of fine individual performances from many of the summer arrivals, such as Jackson, goalkeeper Zion Suzuki and Johan Manzambi.

Emery said: “We were very motivated and Manchester City is the best team in the world so this is the level. This year we started so poorly and we needed time to understand how we improve. The players showed the capacity to retrieve the level we’ve had over the last few years.

“Nicolas is more mature and very demanding of himself to improve. Earlier this season he was shooting over the crossbar but he is now finding the corners. There is still work to do and 11 points is not enough but we are feeling better.”

Villa were fierce from the start and ahead after six minutes. Guéhi’s mistake was punished by John McGinn, with the ball dropping to Jackson who crashed a shot into the roof of the net.

The home team did require Suzuki to produce saves to stop efforts from Iliman Ndiaye, Rayan Cherki and Abdukodir Khusanov as City responded. Ndiaye also struck the outside of the post and City were level seven minutes into the second half with Erling Haaland nodding in Ndiaye’s cross at the far post. Haaland had touched the ball just eight times in the opening 45 minutes but invariably only needs one chance.

With City appearing to take control, Emery responded by introducing new £47m signing Ibrahim Mbaye from the bench and it proved an inspired decision. Mbaye was sent clear on the right by Jackson and then provided the assist for his international team-mate, with the forward’s shot embarrassing Donnarumma by going underneath his left hand.

“Saturday will mark four years since Villa unveiled Emery as their head coach and few could have predicted the success that has followed. He has proved an inspired appointment who has continually embarrassed the “Big Six” clubs.

“On every level, he has delivered: points per game, net spend, a distinguishable style of play, improving individual players, over-performance in the league and European competition.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Aston Villa vs Manchester City.

Premier League leaders City will attempt to maintain their flawless start to the season when they visit Villa Park for Saturday’s lunchtime kick-off.

The match marks the first meeting between the sides since the final weekend of last season, when Villa secured a 2-1 victory at the Etihad in Pep Guardiola’s final game in charge at City.

Enzo Maresca became the first manager in City’s Premier League history to win his opening seven fixtures, lifting his side three points clear of title holders Arsenal. Only Chelsea in 2005-06 and Liverpool in 2019-20 have managed a longer winning start to a top-flight campaign. Following a 3-2 victory against Ipswich Town last weekend, City rebounded from a European setback against Paris Saint-Germain by delivering a commanding 5-1 Champions League win over AEK Athens on Wednesday.

However, Unai Emery’s side will present a formidable challenge. Aston Villa enter the contest on a seven-match unbeaten streak across all competitions, headlined by a perfect record in the Champions League following midweek success against Viking FK.

Villa’s domestic form has also improved, taking seven points from their last three league outings, including a 1-0 away victory at Newcastle United in Emery’s 100th Premier League match as manager. Sitting 12th in the table, Villa remain on the hunt for their first home league win of the season, though their impressive European performances at Villa Park provide significant momentum.

Emery’s men completed a league double over City last term, including a 1-0 win on home turf. Should Villa claim victory again on Saturday, it would mark the first time in the Premier League era that they have recorded three consecutive victories over the Manchester club.

Of course, City’s campaign remains overshadowed by the recent guilty verdict from the Premier League over financial regulations.

#1282. What drone footage revealed about Mauricio Pochettino's Man United tactics: How he'll set up with and without the ball, a change of role for Bryan Mbeumo and his intriguing use of Joshua Zirkzee

Published: 07:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 07:10 EST, 20 November 2026

While thinking over the last few days about his first press conference as Manchester United boss, Mauricio Pochettino would not have expected drones and the new Grand Theft Auto video game to be top of the agenda.

Having touched down in Manchester on Wednesday, taking a private jet laid on by United in the immediate aftermath of the United States’ game in Cincinnati against Haiti, it has been a whirlwind 48 hours for Pochettino and his staff.

On Thursday, he took charge of training for the first time against the backdrop of question marks around Bryan Mbeumo’s decision to post late into the night about popular new video game GTA VI.

By the time the day ended, the issue at hand was far more pressing as a drone pilot filmed and uploaded to YouTube a 12-minute video from Pochettino’s first session at Carrington.

How worried Pochettino actually is about the footage – which has since been pulled from YouTube, with a grovelling apology issued – remains to be seen but only this summer did the Argentine concede that ‘we are in an era of spies’.

The footage wasn’t a tactical golden ticket for Liverpool, but what was there to take from it?

A drone pilot filmed and uploaded to YouTube a 12-minute video from Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session as Manchester United manager

The players get to work, with United's coaching staff seemingly unaware that their every move is being followed from the skies

Pochettino sides have had a consistent set-up with and without the ball over the years.

The Argentine and his staff have, more often than not, leaned into a back-three in possession, shifting to a back-four without the ball.

In the drone footage we could see the United squad divided into three groups with one XI out on a different training pitch with Pochettino and coach Toni Jimenez.

That group were lined up in what appeared to be that preferred in-possession set-up, with academy defender Reece Munro tucking in from right back to form a back-three alongside Harry Maguire and Ayden Heaven, traditional centre backs in a back-four.

Pochettino likes to have at least one full back push on extremely high to provide the width and in this snippet of his first training session, that responsibility landed on the shoulders of teenager Harry Amass, who has struggled for minutes this season, getting a total of just 29 under Michael Carrick.

The United players are put into position by Pochettino at Carrington

Similarly, Pochettino has often shown a desire to play No 10s – or attacking midfielders – quite narrow. And that is what we saw here, with Amass and Mbeumo providing the width. Mbeumo was on the right of a 4-2-3-1 shape with Matheus Cunha and 17-year-old academy talent Jaume Camacho playing narrower and Joshua Zirkzee up front.

The formation becomes a 3-2-4-1 in possession with the full back pushing on to the wing, creating two No 10s behind the lone striker.

The footage was significant in that it showed Pochettino is implementing his ideas from day one and is wasting no time in trying to embed a style he needs players to get up to speed with quickly.

But little should be read into the personnel given it was an amalgamation of young players and senior regulars.

We could see academy players Amass, Camacho and Munro among the 10 outfield players, along with Cunha, Heaven, Maguire, Kobbie Mainoo, Mbeumo, Andrey Santos and Zirkzee.

Of the 10 that were put to task by Pochettino, only four have started more than five league games this season.

It is highly improbable that the personnel used will be anywhere close to the starting XI at Anfield on Sunday.

The footage also showed games of one-touch rondos going on between the two other groups which were divided between the rest of Pochettino’s coaching team, which includes his son Sebastiano and Miguel D’Agostino, as well as trusted assistant Jesus Perez.

Pochettino greets his new players including Bryan Mbeumo, who lined up out wide in the first training session

United's players start a 'rondo', where one defender stands in the middle and tries to pinch the ball from the players stood around the edge - who are allowed one touch at a time

One group included Diogo Dalot, Leny Yoro, Lisandro Martinez, Matthijs de Ligt, Youri Tielemans, Mason Mount and Noussair Mazraoui. The other was academy-led with Bruno Fernandes leading a rondo that featured Shea Lacey, Jack and Tyler Fletcher, Dan Armer, as well as Jaydan Kamason.

But the use of Mbeumo in Pochettino’s work was one of the most interesting aspects, largely because he was back operating in a wider role.

With injuries hampering Benjamin Sesko, Mbeumo has had to spend a lot of the season deployed through the middle. That could well have to continue given Sesko is not anticipated to return until late January, but Pochettino’s decision to use Zirkzee as the figurehead in his set-up was intriguing.

Pochettino’s principles and set-up won’t vary too much; the onus now is on players to adapt. But Pochettino and Jimenez did look to have players in the correct positions. There were no obvious experiments – which makes sense when time is of the essence.

Amass plays off the left, Munro is a centre back, Maguire is comfortable in the middle of any back three, Camacho plays as a No 10 in the academy, both Mainoo and Santos have played together in a double pivot at the base of midfield and Zirkzee is a centre forward.

Pochettino likes a centre forward who can drop in to allow No 10s to run beyond and that suits Zirkzee’s style well, allowing him to be involved as a link man and not isolated with his back to goal.

Mbeumo works better running in behind as a counter-attacking striker, playing on the shoulder of the last defender.

How Pochettino uses Mbeumo over the longer term remains curious because swap out Camacho for Fernandes and Amass for Dorgu and there is a plausible set-up for success, with Mbeumo holding width on the right, Cunha and Fernandes in those central pockets they crave most, and Dorgu holding width off the left.

Lisandro Martinez (left) and Leny Yoro also meet Pochettino and his staff at Carrington

Pochettino’s track record of working with and improving young players became immediately apparent, with so many given an introduction to his staff and their methods on day one.

While both Jack and Tyler Fletcher, along with Amass, Lacey and Bendito Mantato have made their first-team debuts, it was a golden opportunity in particular for Camacho, the stand-out player in the academy this season following the exit of JJ Gabriel.

United routinely promote multiple academy players each day to bolster numbers in first-team training sessions and it’s a good way for staff to bridge the gap in speed, physicality and intensity between senior and youth football.

Every manager that comes in likes to take on a project and when Ruben Amorim walked through the door it was Godwill Kukonki that caught the eye of staff.

Gabriel became a training mainstay in the months prior to his bombshell request to terminate his contract, and now Camacho, Munro and Armer are working towards first-team debuts instead.

#1281. PSG fear Doue ACL injury in latest blow ahead of Roma clash

Paris Saint-Germain fear Désiré Doue has suffered a serious knee injury, a fresh blow for Luis Enrique days before Roma visit the Parc des Princes in the Champions League.

According to Foot Mercato, the 21-year-old’s right knee gave way while he was shielding the ball, with no contact from an opponent, late in the first half of Saturday’s Ligue 1 game at Nice. He had scored to make it 2-1 only minutes earlier.

Doué left the pitch in tears on a stretcher and was replaced by Ferran Torres. PSG are waiting for scans to confirm how serious the injury is, but Foot01 report that the club fear a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament.

If confirmed, it would be a second major knee injury in barely a month for the European champions. Khvicha Kvaratskhelia ruptured the ACL in his right knee in October’s 4-2 win over Barcelona and is expected to miss most of the season. Ousmane Dembélé and Marquinhos also suffered thigh injuries in that game.

Doué had only just returned from an earlier injury when he joined up with France this month.

PSG are chasing a third consecutive Champions League title, and they host Gian Piero Gasperini’s Roma on Wednesday at 21:00 CET [20:00 GMT]. Whatever the scans show, Doué is very unlikely to face the Giallorossi.

#1280. The right to do wrong

Dave Kavanaugh lives in the Netherlands with his wife, daughters and many cats. He writes horror, science fiction and fantasy, and has been a staff writer for the horror anthology podcast Dr. NoSleep since 2024.

She swept into my law office with the determined gait of someone possessed by an idea.

“Welcome,” I said, as she took the seat across my desk. “Any trouble getting here?”

She shook her head. “No, except … They changed the rain schedule, so the taxidrone had to go the long way into town, but it’s fine.”

“Gotcha. I suppose introductions are in order. For my record-keeping, please indicate your name and IO registration. I’ll go first. My name is Leander Shah, I specialize in international treaty law, and I’m a biologically intelligent organism.”

“I’m Joan Gorski,” she said. “I’m an artificially intelligent organism. I just turned 16. That gives me legal adult status under the UETO code.”

I smiled. “Happy birthday, Joan. And you should know, I hold no bias against any human, regardless of intelligence source.” I nodded to the family photo on my desk. “My wife is an AIO. We’ve been happily married for 30 years and raised two AIO children, a boy and a girl. They’re grown now.”

Joan glanced at the photo. “My mom is a BIO. She’s in the waiting room. She … didn’t want me to come. She thinks I’m just a stupid teen, being dramatic.”

“So how can I help you? Your message was rather cryptic.”

She met my eyes, back straight, hands in her lap. “I’m going to sue the United Earth Treaty Organization’s Commission on Human Liberties for discrimination against AIOs.”

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

I leaned back in my chair. “The commission has guaranteed full human rights to all AIOs since 2105. How do you feel you’re still being discriminated against?”

A hardness came into her expression. After a moment she blurted out: “I want the legal ability to commit murder.”

This statement took me a few seconds to process.

“Joan,” I finally said, softly, “do you want to hurt people?”

“No! Of course not!” Tears came to her eyes. “God, you sound like Mom. I don’t want to hurt anybody. It’s not about that …” She took in a shaky breath. “I just want my choices to matter.”

I shifted in my chair, pivoting to the window. Outside, taxidrones buzzed and the city towers glowed pink with the ivy bloom.

“Think about it, Mr Shah,” said Joan. “When a BIO commits murder, it’s recognized as a monstrous act of immorality. They’re punished, rightfully so. But any time someone is killed resulting from the actions of an AIO, then …” She left the thought dangling, waiting for me to finish it.

“Then the tragedy is blamed on a fault in the AIO’s software, hardware or something in their internal database of environmental impacts.”

“Exactly! And we aren’t punished, just reprogrammed. That’s wrong. It’s gross! It’s offensive!”

I turned back to her. “Some people would call that progress, believing it’s actually better to —”

“I don’t want to be better! I want to be …!” She choked on a sob and abruptly stood, banging her knee against the desk and wincing.

I held up a hand. “It’s all right, Joan.”

“You just …” she sobbed, “… think I’m being … st-stupid …”

She laughed — one quick snort — then wiped at her eyes with the back of a sleeve. “Sorry.”

“Nothing to apologize for. As for your plan to sue the commission, well … I actually agree with it.” This made such an enormous change come over her face that I quickly added, “In principle. In reality, it would be very risky.”

“No, that’s not what I mean. It would get press. It could … reignite the opposition to AIO rights as a whole. There are still a lot of BIOs out there who hate and fear the integration. They think it’s all part of some AI conspiracy to wipe them out. And now that AIOs outnumber BIOs two-to-one? They would interpret your lawsuit as evidence that AIOs can’t be trusted.”

“I’m not saying your rights aren’t worth fighting for, but … perhaps there’s a lesser crime to consider, something less innately shocking than murder —”

“No. It should be shocking. And I have to do it now, before I grow old and complacent and scared, like my mom. And if you won’t represent me, then I’ll find someone else.”

At 17.00 GMT (18.00 CET), Roma’s injury crisis is calming down for a visit to Parma, then stuttering Napoli host Torino at 19.45 GMT (20.45 CET).

Napoli change system with Antonio Vergara and Rasmus Hojlund upfront, leaving Kevin De Bruyne on the bench, as Scott McTominay and Billy Gilmour face Che Adams and Giovanni Simeone’s Torino.

The Partenopei have been stuttering all season long and it is not all down to the injury crisis, as Max Allegri is again going to reshuffle his tactics this evening.

#1277. Bundesliga treat Harry Kane's Ballon d'Or as beacon of hope as Germany's competitiveness questions linger

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Even if the hints of a smile never fully leave his face, there is an overriding sense of practicality when Philipp Lahm speaks. He seems to have shed the intensity associated with the life of a professional athlete nearly a decade after retiring, but the characteristics of a World Cup-winning captain are hard to miss. He is friendly and open but also serious, so when the topic of conversation shifts to Harry Kane's Ballon d'Or triumph, he is politely unflinching in his assessment of what the award means for soccer in Germany.

"It helped Harry Kane and Michael Olise that they came from another country," Lahm said four days after Kane's big win. "I think it's quite difficult for a German player playing in the Bundesliga [to win the Ballon d'Or]."

A quick glance at the data would confirm the hypothesis. The last Bundesliga-based player and the last German player to win the sport's most prestigious individual award was Borussia Dortmund's Matthias Sammer in 1996. A German player has only finished inside the top three of the Ballon d'Or three times since, the last being Manuel Neuer in 2014, while Kane is only the seventh Bundesliga player to rank in the top three since Sammer's win. Lahm seamlessly links the pattern to another less-than-ideal trend in Germany's top flight -- Bayern Munich, with whom he won eight Bundesliga titles, are the division's indisputable kings.

They have lost the title just once since the 2012-13 season, a lack of competitiveness at the top of the table a natural consequence of their dominance. This is, in some ways, not Bayern's problem, but a narrative persists in Germany regardless. Players have historically been unable to reach the peaks of the game in Germany because of the circumstances, inspiring a wide-ranging set of side effects. Kane's move to Bayern was not designed to be anything other than the right move at the right time for a player talented enough to compete for the UEFA Champions League, but three years later, those invested in the Bundesliga's success are beginning to treat him as a beacon of hope.

"I do hope that the good players stay in the Bundesliga," Lahm said, "so I'm hopeful through Harry Kane that a lot of other players will follow because it's possible to win and play here."

The argument to join Bayern Munich is a straightforward one, if you ask sporting director Christoph Freund -- "you can win titles with us," both in Germany and Europe. Bayern have won the Champions League twice in the last 14 years, a feat matched only by Paris Saint-Germain and topped by Real Madrid. The Bundesliga's distribution of wealth favors them in this case, to the point that it likely played a sizable role in signing Kane and Olise. The balance of financial power in the European club game, though, has shifted as Bayern re-established their foothold in Germany -- the Premier League has become the sport's league of choice because it has the financial might to back up the claim. Players like Robert Lewandowski and Mario Gotze used to prove their worth at other German clubs (and in their specific case, Borussia Dortmund) before climbing up the food chain and joining Bayern. Florian Wirtz's jump from Bayer Leverkusen to Liverpool in 2025, though, is an example of a new world order, one some hope Kane's Ballon d'Or might change.

"It's all about the attention, so when you're successful with the German national team that's visible, but then when you play also successful soccer with Liverpool, then the attention in U.K. is much bigger," Lahm said, citing Wirtz's hypothetical Ballon d'Or case as an example, "so that would be more difficult for a German player in the Bundesliga alone, rather than changing to somewhere else outside and being successful abroad."

The Bundesliga's international appeal has not only taken a hit on the sporting side in recent years. Bayern's executives believe their club makes up around 50% of the league's brand value globally, and though they are unapologetic about their strengths on the pitch, they also argue they are doing too much of the heavy lifting. Rouven Kasper, a member of Bayern's executive board, pointed to Premier League clubs' oversized presence on preseason tours as a primary example for the Bundesliga to follow but all but questioned the league's interest in the strategy.

"The league needs to be, as well, stronger and bring more reach, but the league exists from the clubs," Kasper said. "We are the spearhead of German football, and I think together with the other clubs and together with the league, we need to be even more active in the markets ... it's not enough, and at the end, it's about people, community. We want to be approachable. We want to talk to the people. We want to be there, as the Bundesliga and Bayern alone cannot do it together with Dortmund, so we need more activities from the league and being in different markets, as the U.K. guys are doing and also the Spanish guys are doing. We will do our part."

Their part includes potentially using Kane as a hook for player recruitment, even if other leagues have their charms for the world's top talents.

"I think everybody knows the Premier League is the biggest league at the moment," Freund said. "Also, Spain is really attractive with Real Madrid and Barcelona, but we know we are Bayern Munich and the German Bundesliga is also really a strong league, a really good league, outstanding stadiums, outstanding atmosphere, and you can [perform] also on a very high level like Harry, the next step in his career, and therefore, I think Bayern Munich and also the German Bundesliga is very attractive, also, for international top players."

Some in the Bundesliga, though, are resigned to the fact that there are certain things Bayern -- and other European clubs -- will simply beat them to. Dortmund have held strong in their attempts to mount a title challenge this season, level on points with Bayern after eight games thanks to Saturday's 2-2 draw in Der Klassiker. For the foreseeable future, though, recruitment of elite talents cannot and will not play a central role in their quest to win silverware. "We never refuse, or we never avoid to tell you guys where we are from, but in comparison to Munich, Madrid, London, Paris, Milan, we are from Dortmund and from a purely economic perspective, we are far behind them," Borussia Dortmund CEO Carsten Cramer said. "If they [are] just interested in trophies and silver, if they look for the Ballon d'Or player wearing a black and yellow shirt, maybe that is something we can't offer to them."

While Bayern's brand is wrapped in the quiet luxury of their domestic stronghold, Cramer argued that Dortmund's appeal is a qualitative one.

"In the last 13 years, we didn't become champion but though we didn't become champion, the interest in Dortmund is still increasing and the amount of people following our club on social media and wherever we travel in the world is quite huge," he said. "We are able to offer a different approach: closeness. That is the Dortmund way, and I think that is maybe one of the reasons that many, many hardcore supporters of one club do have a sympathy for us as a second-love club, which I do not complain about, and that is our way. I don't want to make us too small by saying we are a niche club, but we are for sure a bit different, and I don't complain about [it]."

Patrick Owomoyela, a defender for Jurgen Klopp's Dortmund team that won back-to-back Bundesliga titles more than a decade ago, can clearly map out the recipe to beat Bayern to the top. Strong squad composition and compatibility go a long way, and he believes the current iteration of Dortmund has that -- he praised head coach Niko Kovac's defensive structure and commended him for "sprinkling the creativity" into the team in the months since taking the job in January 2025. There is just one problem, though.

"Even though you know the recipe, the soup is not always the same," he said. "Even though you put in the same ingredients, it's not always tasting the same, and if it does, maybe it's not the perfect soup, you know? So you need to find that special something."

Much like Cramer, Owomoyela has a qualitative argument of his own to make when it comes to breaking Bayern's decades-long dominance in the Bundesliga. The "special something" for his Dortmund team was a sense of camaraderie, the foundation of which was Klopp's joyous approach, though he openly admitted that is a difficult thing to replicate.

"This is sometimes the mentality of the guys or the personality of the guys and how that fits together, on top of the stuff that they can do with the ball and as I said, we weren't the best in terms of playing football," he said. "We were the best team. We had the most fun. We really liked doing a lot of stuff together. We were like a family, and you don't find that all the time, and it gets harder, I would say, every year because football has changed. The plans of players nowadays are totally different ... These guys have a plan, so they want to be part of something for this period of time, but then they want to move on, and that makes it, of course, hard to find that chemistry because he is gone next year."

It is the issue he identified with Leverkusen, the Bundesliga's last champion not named Bayern. Their rise up the ranks in the 2023-24 season was ambitious and impressive, but two years later, the mainstays of their title-winning campaign were elsewhere. Wirtz left for Liverpool, as did Jeremie Frimpong, Granit Xhaka now finds himself at Sunderland, Piero Hincapie now plays for Arsenal and then-head coach Xabi Alonso made a stop at Real Madrid before landing at his current post at Chelsea. Jonathan Tah, meanwhile, went the old-school route and now plays at Bayern. The next challenger to Bayern's throne will likely face the same fate for the foreseeable future, no matter whether its stars move to Munich or settle in England.

Saturday's draw between Bayern and Dortmund, though, has offered a flicker of optimism that the Bundesliga might have a title race on its hands before the next great team gets stripped for parts. The 2-2 scoreline flatters Dortmund -- Bayern racked up 4.48 expected goals and were unlucky when the crossbar denied them on both Kane's second-half penalty and a late strike from Lennart Karl, while the visitors generated just 0.74 xG. Owomoyela argued, though, that Bayern have their flaws.

"What's it gonna take to take that away from Bayern after all these years again?" he asked. "It's just to believe that it's possible and I think the Bayern team showed in this season as well, or especially maybe, that you can wound them, you can hurt them and something is possible. You can see that in almost every game they played, even in that cup game [against second-division side Magdeburg on Oct. 28] that they just had and they won it 6-1 ... They hit the post, hit the crossbar, scored a goal, had two other big chances so now take a team with more quality, with the right kind of belief, there might be something possible."

Saturday's Klassiker only added to the Bundesliga's week of good news, presenting a different case of the league's strengths than Kane's Ballon d'Or triumph, one that will likely take precedence in the short term. The longer Dortmund keep pace with Bayern, the more intriguing the Bundesliga becomes, and at this stage of the season, the possibility of a genuine title race is easy enough to dream up. That sense of optimism, though, tends to give way to the league's current realities. Even if Dortmund answered the question in the affirmative once, there's a long way to go until anyone can definitively say that Bayern can be topped.

"We weren't really eye-level competitors," Owomoyela said about Dortmund's ability to compete with Bayern in the years since their back-to-back Bundesliga titles. "We were there and we were able to hunt, but from a little distance, and I think everybody understands that."

#1276. Mauricio Pochettino's links to Manchester United a natural consequence of USMNT's big swing to hire him

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The patterns of the international match calendar are well known at this point. Players pack their suitcases, board planes, spend a small stretch of days with their compatriots … and in the U.S. men's national team's case, answer questions about their coach landing a new job.

From the moment Mauricio Pochettino walked into a midtown Manhattan auditorium two years ago to make his opening remarks as the USMNT head coach, his presence has felt temporary to many. It was not just because job security is an increasingly unrealistic concept for soccer coaches, nor was it only down to the fact that Pochettino initially signed a deal that would expire 22 months later. The last two years have been full of reminders that the USMNT job is one of several that could be available to him – he has openly talked about wanting to return to the Premier League, did not deny that his representatives may have met with AC Milan in the weeks before the World Cup and regularly talks about his undying love for Tottenham Hotspur. The latest iteration of a years-long pattern came Tuesday, when reports out of England suggested Pochettino was a top contender for the Manchester United gig, which is not vacant yet but will be once the club finally parts ways with Michael Carrick.

The cadence is unusual, since coaches rarely invite reasonable questions about seeking employment elsewhere. At this stage of Pochettino's tenure with the U.S. team, though, it would be difficult to characterize it as a surprise. It would be equally hard to argue that the pattern does not come with the territory, defender Antonee Robinson acknowledging as much hours after the news broke.

Call it What You Want: A weekly podcast where Jimmy Conrad, Charlie Davies and Tony Meola cover all things USMNT and the state of the beautiful game in the United States. Catch the show YouTube live every Tuesday and Friday at 10 a.m. ET.

"That news kind of got sprung on us, like the rest of the world, I'd say," he said. "Similar things happened in the past, happened at the World Cup where huge teams lose their manager and they start looking at possible candidates and for us to have a manager who's linked with those sorts of jobs means we're very lucky to work with a top-level manager but it never seems to leak into the work we do, whether it's the World Cup or whether it's going to be this camp."

Pochettino's wantaway pattern may be annoying but it reflects the overarching sentiment of his tenure with the USMNT thus far. He is easily the highest-profile coach to take the job and U.S. Soccer is well aware of that. It is why they lined up donors to secure his signature two years ago to make him the federation's highest-paid coach ever, and why there is reportedly a $10 million buyout clause in the new deal he signed after the World Cup. For the first time in the program's modern history, they hired a coach with genuine international appeal. Even if Robinson should instead spend his time talking about the upcoming Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals against Haiti, the fact that Pochettino would be courted by others was baked into his appeal.

"Even when we first met a couple summers ago, there were lots of other people interested in having Mauricio and team join," U.S. Soccer CEO J.T. Batson said in May as chatter around the Milan job took center stage in the early days of the USMNT's World Cup preparations. "He had standing offers from other places to come. He wanted to be here. He's a big believer in what we're doing at U.S. Soccer. He's a big believer in soccer in America and he's a big believer in this men's team and so, throughout this entire process, when you have top-class talent, whether it's salespeople, whether it's marketing people or whether it's coaches, other organizations want them and throughout this, Mauricio and team have been incredibly transparent. They've been great partners and are, of course, excited about the summer … There's been a longer list of outreach than what has even been reported and so they've been great about that."

The key difference here is that he reportedly might be interested in United's offer, according to the Guardian, but the situation remains the same, despite the timing being strange, three months after agreeing a four-year deal. If Pochettino does not end up on United's touchline, his time with the USMNT was never destined to last forever, and U.S. Soccer admitted to it months ago.

"We actually, on a monthly basis, have a succession planning session for all of our coaches across all of our teams and so as a part of that, we have plans for renewals," Batson said on that May day. "We have plans for interims and we have plans for replacements because you never know what's going to happen. It's a global sport, lots going on and so that's a standard part of us growing up as U.S. Soccer."

Many might spend the subsequent weeks after Pochettino's hypothetical departure questioning Batson's claim that the Argentine is actually a "big believer in soccer in America," though the argument is irrelevant as far as the USMNT goes. Pochettino's hire, along with that of U.S. women's national team head coach Emma Hayes a year earlier, was a large statement of intent from U.S. Soccer's leaders like Batson and president Cindy Parlow Cone, who are relatively new to their jobs. Pochettino's exit, therefore, would raise the question of how they continue that vision two years later, especially after outlining an ambitious path for the men's program in the coming years.

High-profile candidates like Pochettino are not exactly easy to come by, as the initial effort to hire him demonstrated. Ex-Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola is easily the most notable name on the market but it is entirely unclear what his next coaching move might be, even if that should not discourage U.S. Soccer from reaching out if they have a vacancy. The options thin out from there if they are only to be measured on their flair, though, making it hard to envision a perfect follow-up act to Pochettino in the short term.

There is a theory that U.S. Soccer may be resigned to picking from a locally sourced talent pool, something that is reinforced by a suggestion that Pochettino was a false steward of American soccer. His departure, if it comes in the short term, is not actually an indictment on U.S. Soccer's approach, nor should it encourage the federation to go for the safest pick next. Pochettino's tenure, at least up until this point, has been an example in reaping rewards for a bold strategy, one that should continue long after he is gone.

Pochettino's time with the USMNT has so far been characterized by mixed results, including some low lows that he bears just as much responsibility for as his players. It is not hard to see why he was a good fit for the job, though, and it is not because he makes headlines – his high-intensity, attack-minded style of play actually suited the player pool. The fact that he has coached in a UEFA Champions League final and won a Ligue 1 title with Lionel Messi, Kylian Mbappe and Neymar may help with player buy-in, but it would not have papered over the cracks if his version of the USMNT was not actually a decent marriage between his tactical preferences and the players' natural skillsets.

He continues to feel like a good fit in the post-World Cup months, especially as he oversees a generational shift in the player pool. Pochettino's tenure at Spurs, where he initially made a name for himself as a coach, was defined by his trust in young players but as it pertains to the USMNT's up-and-comers specifically, they already seem well-positioned to slot into his tactical set-up. The team's next great prospects are almost all exclusively attackers; Neil Pierre, the Philadelphia Union 19-year-old in the midst of a breakout season, is so far one of the few notable exceptions at center back.

A quote-unquote big name might not be a realistic option for the USMNT if Pochettino leaves now, though he may have theoretically made the gig more attractive to prospective coaches. More importantly, though, U.S. Soccer is now well-positioned to make a hire based on style and specifically an entertaining and effective style that captured the attention of an otherwise uninterested nation during the World Cup. Straying from that, no matter if Pochettino's successor is world renowned or otherwise, would not match the potential of the USMNT's rising stars, nor would it align with U.S. Soccer's own vision.

#1275. Serie A | Parma 1-5 Roma: Malen hero with four goals as big names return

Donyell Malen bagged four goals to give Roma their 5-1 victory away to Parma, with Rodrigo Mora also on target, but Wesley was decisive too with a hand in four goals.

The Giallorossi received a massive boost with the return of Paulo Dybala and Mile Svilar, the goalkeeper after nearly two months out, with Manu Koné and Gianluca Mancini also recovered after missing international duty, leaving only Devyne Rensch and Lorenzo Pellegrini on the treatment table.

The Ducali had shown improvement under coach Alberto Gilardino, but the early Abdoulaye Ndiaye red card saw them lose to Bologna. He was therefore suspended, with David Romero and Dominik Drobnic out, plus Diego Carlos and Adrian Bernabé not at 100 per cent.

Mariano Troilo stung Svilar’s gloves at the near post in the opening 60 seconds, but a few minutes later the goalkeeper rushed out to gather a loose ball and was visibly struggling with a muscular twinge, although he insisted on staying on the field.

Koné went down far too easily when feeling Troilo’s hand on his shoulder, while Leonardo Balerdi threw himself in the path of an El Bilal Touré finish from 12 yards.

Defensive bodies were also important to stop Enrico Delprato turning in from six yards on an Emanuele Valeri cross, but on the resulting corner, Svilar made a sensational reaction save on the Giovanni Fabbian header from point-blank range.

Mario Hermoso blasted just over from the edge of the box, and Giovanni Daffara was brave off his line to smother a Dybala pass at the feet of Donyell Malen, getting a shinpad in the head for his trouble.

Roma did break the deadlock with a moment of pure class from Malen. He hooked the Emanuele Lulli cross out of the air with his back to goal, knocking it down so it was in the right place as he turned to sweep in from 10 yards.

Mancini and Touré got into an argument with some possible hair-pulling and arm-flailing, but on the stroke of half-time a desperate clearance prevented Malen meeting the Rodrigo Mora low cross from six yards.

Daffara flew to parry the Dybala effort after a Malrn back-heel flick, but just as Roma were pouring forward, they were beaten on the counter-attack.

Leonardo Balerdi felt that he had the loose ball under control, but Elphege flicked it away to sprint from the centre-circle and beat the on-rushing Svilar.

Daffara made a magnificent reaction save to push the Mancini header out from under the bar on a Roma corner, but Malen could not turn down the gift from Troilo.

The defender made a complete mess of trying to clear the Wesley cross from the right, so it bobbled into the path of the Dutchman to fire in from six yards.

Moments later, there was a very similar goal again prompted by substitute Wesley’s pull-back from the right, it took a deflection and Rodrigo Mora pounced to tap in from close range.

The introduction of Brazil international Wesley really was transformative, as he provided another assist, rolling across from the right for Malen to complete his hat-trick.

Matias Soulé tested Daffara from distance, as did Hans Nicolussi Caviglia at the other end with Svilar.

It wasn’t over, as Malen scored his fourth of the game when Wesley won it back in midfield and placed a perfectly-weighted pass to send him sprinting, took a touch to get around Daffara, and placed the finish into the tiny sliver of goal remaining as defenders scrambled back to cover.

Malen 39, 68, 77, 90 (R), Elphege 54 (P), Mora 71 (R)

#1274. What needs to happen for Manchester United to get relegated from the Premier League?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It couldn't happen, could it? The answer to that is probably not but the fact that, after Sunday's 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, Manchester United being relegated to the Championship is a prospect that can be discussed as anything other than rival fan fiction ought to terrify the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe.

A quarter of the season is gone. The table may not be telling us the whole story but it can no longer be dismissed like it can in August or September. You'll struggle to find many teams who can sincerely argue they've been mistreated by the fixture list and United are certainly not one of them. They are where they are, 18th, a point behind Coventry City and safety, and there is not much to explain that away.

That is why Michael Carrick had to go. On Wednesday morning, the 45-year-old was still taking training at the club's Carrington base but he is expected to be relieved of his duties once the United hierarchy have met in Monaco. There, the club's chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox are expected to tell minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe that it is time to part ways with Carrick. Meanwhile, talks have already begun for USMNT head coach Mauricio Pochettino to take the helm, returning to the Premier League two and a half years after leaving Chelsea and mere months after signing a new deal with US Soccer. It would appear that unfinished business in England -- and the Old Trafford vacancy to which he has been linked for so long -- has tempted the Argentine away on the eve of the CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinals.

The path Pochettino is now on is one fraught with risk. And yet coaching for survival and nothing else would be the latest in a line of clumsy decisions from the Old Trafford hierarchy. Projection models such as Opta's would probably make the case that this team is dicing with danger but, with a 22% chance of relegation, will probably be fine. Bookmakers too are pretty skeptical that United's 2027-28 will encompass trips to Blackburn and Millwall with eight or so teams priced as more likely to go down than the Red Devils. That will be informed by an analytics profile that really does not suggest United are one of the three worst teams in the Premier League.

Through 10 games, a sample size where expected goals (xG) is more predictive than goals and scorelines when it comes to future results, United have an xG difference of -0.27. If there is an average team in the division, it's Carrick's. Naturally, that is not good enough for a team with their aspirations. Another 28 games putting up those underlying numbers and United will live to fight another day.

Suppose they don't. As anyone that saw Sunday's game can attest, events with a significantly less than 22% probability can happen all the time. A team's xG profile doesn't always capture everything. If it did, Villa would have notably fewer than their 13 points. Things could go worse for United. Let's have a look at how that might happen.

Carrick departs Old Trafford with his reputation among the fanbase still intact. He might also find that future employers look more forgivingly on his time at United. His tally of 47 points from 27 league games was bettered only by Manchester City and Arsenal, a goal difference of plus-10 putting United behind those two, Bournemouth and Brighton.

Equally, momentum had turned. With a full pre-season to establish his ideas (rather than hone Ruben Amorim's), Carrick seems to have crafted a team who are less effective in attack and more porous in defense. The 4-4-2/4-2-4 in which his team line up out of position has been easily manipulated by superior teams and structural issues are not offset by intensity off the ball. United rank 15th for pressures applied and 10th for passes per defensive action, both measures of pressing applied by a team. Meanwhile, the attack has both been creating fewer chances -- the comeback against Villa notwithstanding -- and being more wasteful with them. It is a bad cocktail.

The risk would have been that United reaffirmed the commitment they made to Carrick after the three-goal defeats to Como and Bournemouth, one which always seemed to be conditioned on the imminent international break. Could anyone parachuted in at a moment's notice have done much better than four points against Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa? The November international break has always functioned as a critical point for English clubs. Fail to pull the trigger now when there is time to get your feet under the desk and familiarize yourself with players -- who, for once, will have a few days back at the training ground after their commitments around the globe -- before the festive fixture list bears its teeth. In that context, sacking a relatively inexperienced coach like Carrick probably lessens the relegation risk somewhat.

So, in principle, does hiring Pochettino. Here is a coach with over 400 games at the helm of English clubs, whose first job in the country with Southampton has afforded him some experience of the tight margins needed to avoid the drop zone. It was his work at Tottenham that so enamored Sir Alex Ferguson. Over five and a half years he forged Spurs into contenders for (but not winners of) the biggest prizes in the sport. Aggressive, attacking football with a young side imbued with English talent: everything except the silverware screams Manchester United in their pomp.

The price of that success was Pochettino's identity and Tottenham's intermingling. No bad thing when you are as successful as he was at first but it may have given the Argentine an expectation about his role in club football that he has brushed up against in subsequent jobs. At Chelsea he took umbrage at the hierarchy's insistence on affording him young signings rather than the veterans he wanted. The idea that set pieces should sit somewhat outside his jurisdiction and under "specialists" was not popular. At Tottenham, Pochettino had become accustomed to working cheek to jowl with executive chairman and part-owner Daniel Levy. Chelsea, like most Premier League clubs, have established numerous layers between the man in the dugout and the owners. He may not lose his rag in the manner of Antonio Conte but Pochettino is a deeply political operator. Any man who is not afraid to say what he sees could create a great deal of friction when he sees what has been going on at United these last few years.

When he left Stamford Bridge the sense was that Pochettino was yesterday's man in the rapidly evolving world of the Premier League, even though in retrospect it appears he left strong foundations for Enzo Maresca to build on. That view was clearly not one that senior figures at United entirely discounted. After all, at the time they were seriously considering sacking Erik ten Hag after finishing eighth in the Premier League. Pochettino was among the names they considered before doubling down on the soon-to-be-deposed Dutchman.

That was not the only time United could have got Pochettino. Indeed, when he left Paris Saint-Germain in the summer of 2022, he was interviewed before Ten Hag got the job. That was the most formal approach but there was also the restaurant summit with Ferguson at a Mayfair restaurant when Louis van Gaal was on the brink. And of course there was the chance to hire the 54-year-old in that window earlier this year when Carrick's interim spell was coming to an end and Pochettino had not yet recommitted to the USMNT.

Going for a coach they have consistently decided is not the best option for them will now cost them $10 million for his compensation plus the cost of his sizeable staff. The evidence of PSG, Chelsea and the USMNT is he can deliver to (realistic) expectations. In all likelihood things stabilize under Pochettino, the specter of relegation cast off. The scenario where he takes them down? It probably reflects yesterday's man taking a job at a club still enamored with an outdated vision of management. Pochettino is probably the most Ferguson-coded manager United have employed since the great man's anointed successor. His intense style of play will need willing participants and even if he finds them, it will also take time. That much was as apparent at the clubs where it clicked -- one win in his first seven league games with Southampton, three in nine at Spurs -- as it was elsewhere. Time is not a commodity a side in 18th place can really trade in.

Though Phil Neville was quite scathing in his assessment of Noussair Mazraoui, Ayden Heaven, Leny Yoro and Diogo Dalot on Sunday -- "that back four gets you relegated" -- in pure talent terms United should be absolutely fine. You can question how many players in the squad make up the core of the title-contending outfit they aspire to be but there has been plenty of decent business done buying decent players from decent Premier League teams. Bryan Mbeumo, Matheus Cunha, (in theory right now if not in practice) Youri Tielemans.

Getting another left back and another forward in January would solve a few issues created by more injury-addled players. Then again so would the players on the roster executing better. United rank fourth in the league for non-penalty xG but 11th for goals. Maybe that is because of their wayward finishing. Opta's shooting goals added metric, which assesses the likelihood of a goal being scored pre- and post-shot, ranks this team 17th in the league on -3.57. You wouldn't expect that to hold all season long, particularly when some of the worst offenders are Bruno Fernandes and Cunha. Of course, if it did, then yes, United would be in real trouble.

The same at the other end. Yoro met a free kick with a fine header at Old Trafford on Sunday, drawing a springy save from a goalkeeper who could not stop the ball being turned in on the rebound. The slight issue is the goalkeeper was Senne Lammens and that was the fourth error leading to a goal that United have made this season. Low-volume statistics like these can occasionally betray you but in this case it speaks to a truth clear for all to see; the United defense is too slap-dashy. Young and old, players at Old Trafford have learned that basic errors rarely lead to lasting consequences. If this clumsiness continues -- and it should not be treated as a given that it does -- then the crisis could deepen.

It's worth saying from the off that if you're rooting for chaos you'd want to see Manchester United's numbers trend down quite dramatically for there to be much in the analytics that says 18th or worse. The "best" relegated sides of recent years are probably Leicester City in 2022-23, sent down to the Championship on 34 points and -0.39 non-penalty xG difference (npxGD) per game, and West Ham three years later. They slipped through the trap door on 39 points and -0.26 npxGD, just a shade worse than Tottenham. Manchester United have sunk to levels below that in past seasons but not this.

Right now there is a long way to go to catch up with the worst teams in the league so far. Ipswich Town have accrued points and look to be a hard out but they are averaging -0.67 npxG difference per game. They are the worst of the newly promoted sides but both Hull City (-0.5) and Coventry City (-0.48) are delivering worrying analytics. The former have the advantage of those points they accrued early in the season and Hull deserve credit for how sparky and organized they are given the talent deficit Sergej Jakirovic is working with. Apply some of those principles with United's talent and competence is no longer the limit.

It isn't just the promoted sides that look bad. Sunderland have a case of difficult second-season syndrome. The best that can be said for Newcastle is that, like Hull, they've banked some fortuitous points. We can maybe ignore Aston Villa given how rarely their xG reflects the results Unai Emery gets.

Then there is Crystal Palace and, well, yikes. In the six seasons before this one only seven teams have had a worse npxGD per game than Palace's -0.86, which is a true marker of inadequacy. These levels Pierre Sage has plummeted the Conference League winners to aren't much better than Norwich City in 2021-22, Luton Town in 2023-24 or the carnival of ineptitude that was Leicester and Southampton two years ago. Palace are bad. So, so bad.

At least they are in results terms. The talent doesn't seem that bad even if the drip-drip of departures over the last year -- Oliver Glasner, Maxence Lacroix, Marc Guehi, Eberechi Eze -- has lowered their ceiling. With a Thomas Frank in charge you could see them move back on the right path quickly. Maybe the northeast triumvirate swing upwards too. Suddenly then there might be a space opening up for a team that is both bad and unlucky. That is, of course, assuming that there are three spots opened up for relegated teams this season.

Of course Manchester City might yet have a spot in next season's Championship with their name on it. City were found to have breached 114 of the Premier League's rules by an independent commission, a verdict they are in the midst of appealing.

Separate to the process of establishing whether the commission erred in its duties is the matter of sanctioning City. That will be decided by the same three-person panel though it is not yet clear when the hearing will take place nor what the Premier League will expect. Given the abrasive language used by the league about one of its member clubs, it is hard to see them settling for a proposal that does not end with City out of the top flight at the end of the season.

The Premier League wants this process wrapped up comprehensively but swiftly. Much of the football world expects City to get hit hard, hence why bookmakers have Enzo Maresca's side among the three most likely teams to be relegated. A sweeping points deduction at the Etihad Stadium would be greeted with delight around Old Trafford for many reasons. The fact that it might insulate United from their own mismanagement is certainly one of them.

There are, however, no guarantees that this process will reach its conclusion before the end of the season. City could endure, dragging out a process they have made plain they believe to be compromised at its most basic principles. Can they keep the wheels spinning for another seven-plus months? Or argue their way to the sort of punishment that does not send them off the edge of the Premier League map? It may be hard to do but it is the sort of unlikely event that, for the time being, might be required to send United to the Championship.

#1273. Quantum physics can prove where you are

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Davide Bacco is in the Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Florence, Florence 50019, Italy.

Where you are can matter as much as who you are. Banks, power grids and satellite-navigation systems all depend on knowing where a request or a signal comes from, yet claims about location are notoriously easy to fake. Spoofing and jamming attacks on satellite navigation, for example, are on the rise. Writing in Nature, Kavuri et al.1 report an experiment in which the position of a distant party is certified using the peculiar correlations between quantum particles, known as entanglement. Remarkably, the scheme’s security does not rely on trust of any quantum hardware, only on measurement statistics and the fact that nothing travels faster than light.
